items.q: **Explain the concept of customer relationship management. How can technology help here? What are the benefits of CRM?**
items.answer:
**Definition:**
- **CRM is a strategy for managing a company's interactions with its customers and sales prospects**
- **Often CRM is equated with automating business processes related to sales, marketing and customer service — but CRM is not just about technology**
- **It involves strategy and redesign of business processes**, with the goal to **find, attract and win new customers, retain those customers, and finally get feedback from them to better design the company's product and customer facing processes**

> **"CRM is not just about technology" is the single most examinable sentence in this chapter** — and it is exactly Unit 2's argument about ERP itself. **A company that installs a CRM but keeps its sales people hoarding contacts in personal notebooks has bought a database nobody fills in.**

**The goal statement is a four-stage life cycle**, and reading it that way makes the whole chapter fall into place:

$$\textbf{find} \rightarrow \textbf{attract and win} \rightarrow \textbf{retain} \rightarrow \textbf{learn from}$$

| Stage | Which application serves it |
|---|---|
| **find** | Marketing Management |
| **attract and win** | Sales Force Automation |
| **retain** | Call Centre · Field Service |
| **learn from** | CRM Analytics |

**The last stage is the one people forget** — feedback *"to better design the company's product and customer facing processes"* means **CRM is an input to product design**, which is what makes it a strategy rather than a sales tool.

---

**How technology helps:**
- **CRM uses people, processes, and technology to gain insight into the behavior of customers**
- **CRM can bring together information from all data sources within an organization (and from outside, like social media) to give one holistic view of the customer in real time**
- **It allows customer facing employees from sales, customer support and marketing to make informed decisions on everything from cross selling and upselling opportunities to target marketing strategies to competitive positioning tactics**
- **CRM can also reduce the costs of marketing, sales and customer service**

**"One holistic view of the customer" is the central claim.** Without it, the same customer exists as several different customers:

| Department | What they know |
|---|---|
| **Sales** | the deals, the pipeline, discount history |
| **Support** | the complaints, the open tickets |
| **Marketing** | which campaigns they responded to |
| **Finance** | what they owe and how late they pay |

**The failure mode is concrete:** a salesperson calls to upsell a customer who has an **unresolved support complaint and an overdue invoice** — because the salesperson cannot see either.

$$\textbf{fragmented customer data} \Rightarrow \textbf{the company contradicts itself in front of the customer}$$

**This is Unit 1's information-silo problem moved from the factory to the customer** — Nestlé's *29 different vanilla records* is the same defect. **ERP unified the internal view; CRM unifies the customer view** — and adds *"from outside the organization if needed, like social media"*, which ERP never claimed. **Note "in real time":** a nightly-batch view is not enough when the customer is on the phone now.

---

**The eight benefits:**
1. **Better profitability / revenue per customer**
2. **Improved Customer Service / Satisfaction**
3. **Higher Productivity**
4. **Focused Marketing**
5. **Better Cross Sell / Up Sell**
6. **Better Opportunity Close**
7. **Reduced Sales and Marketing Expenses**
8. **Increased Customer Retention / Loyalty**

**They form four pairs — a revenue benefit and a cost benefit at each funnel stage:**

| Stage | **Earn more** | **Spend less** |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaching people** | Focused Marketing | Reduced Sales and Marketing Expenses |
| **Winning them** | Better Opportunity Close | Higher Productivity |
| **Growing them** | Cross Sell / Up Sell · profitability per customer | — |
| **Keeping them** | Retention / Loyalty | Improved Customer Service |

**Focused marketing and reduced marketing expense are the same mechanism seen twice** — if you know who is likely to buy, you **stop spending on the ones who are not.**

**"Better profitability per customer" is listed first and is the most strategic**, because it reframes a customer as **a stream of revenue over years** rather than a transaction — which is what justifies spending on retention at all.

⚠️ **Distinguish cross-sell from up-sell:** **cross-sell** = a *different* product *(you bought a laptop; here is a printer)*; **up-sell** = a *better version* of the same thing *(consider the 16GB model)*. **Both are cheap revenue compared with acquiring a new customer, and both require the single customer view to work at all.**

items.q: **What are the different application areas in CRM? Explain each in brief. What is sales force automation, and how do SFA applications help the sales team?**
items.answer:
**CRM Application Areas** — the deck's diagram names ten: **Sales Force Automation · Marketing · Field Service · e-Commerce · Call Centre · Partner Relationship Mgmt · Revenue and Pricing · Product Configuration · Order Management · CRM Analytics**

**Sort them by which funnel stage they serve and the set stops looking arbitrary:**

| Funnel stage | Applications |
|---|---|
| **Find** | **Marketing Management** |
| **Win** | **SFA · Product Configuration · Revenue and Pricing · Order Management** |
| **Serve and keep** | **Call Centre · Field Service** |
| **Sell through others** | **Partner Relationship Management** |
| **Sell without people** | **e-Commerce** |
| **Understand all of it** | **CRM Analytics** |

**Two are structurally different from the rest:** **PRM** is CRM applied to **channel partners rather than end customers**, and **e-Commerce** is the channel where **the customer does the selling to themselves.**

**Brief descriptions:**

| Application | What it does |
|---|---|
| **SFA** | helps the sales force in their daily jobs; **increases productivity** |
| **e-Commerce** | **buy, sell and transact over the Web** — search, cart, promotion, personalization, cross/up-sell, configuration, multichannel ordering, self service |
| **Call Centre** | **answers customer queries and routes calls to the most competent person** |
| **Marketing Management** | end-to-end from **gathering and analyzing customer data** through **planning, budgeting, executing communications** to **measuring results** |
| **Field Service** | **after-sales installation, service, repairs**; **scheduling workforce**, spares, reverse logistics |
| **PRM** | **manage relationships with channel partners** and optimize sales opportunity |
| **Revenue and Pricing** | **optimize and manage prices throughout the product life cycle** — initial, promotional, markdown |
| **Product Configuration** | **customers configure a product to their specification on the web**; sales can then quote quickly |
| **CRM Analytics** | **sales, marketing and customer service analytics** |

---

**Sales Force Automation — the QnA's own answer:**

- **SFA applications help the sales force in their daily jobs and are aimed at increasing their productivity**
- **With these applications, the sales force need not remember or store contact information of thousands of the company's existing customers and new prospects**
- **SFA applications help them to manage new leads and sales opportunities**
- **These applications help the sales force in managing sales in their territory and tracking sales performance, based on which they are provided incentive / compensation**

**Typical areas:** **contact management · lead management / opportunity management · sales forecasting and pipeline · sales performance management · territory management · quote generation.** *(Web 2.0 is gaining popularity among SFA vendors.)*

**Each capability solves one specific problem a salesperson has:**

| Capability | The problem |
|---|---|
| **Contact management** | *"need not remember contact information of **thousands**"* |
| **Lead / opportunity management** | which of my many possible deals deserves my time today? |
| **Sales forecasting and pipeline** | what will I actually close this quarter? |
| **Territory management** | which accounts are mine, and which are a colleague's? |
| **Sales performance management** | what did I achieve — **and therefore what am I paid?** |
| **Quote generation** | a correct, priced proposal without a week of internal chasing |

> **The most important consequence is stated obliquely: *"tracking sales performance, based on which they are provided incentive / compensation."***

**That is why sales people actually use the system.** An SFA that only helps management see the pipeline gets filled in reluctantly and badly. **An SFA that computes commission gets filled in accurately and on time** — because the salesperson has a direct financial stake in its correctness.

**This is the classic adoption lesson**, and it echoes Unit 4's failure factor: *"without user acceptance, even if the system goes LIVE, it will never be used by end users."* **Systems get used when the user, not the manager, benefits.**

⚠️ **Territory management sounds administrative and is really about conflict.** Without a defined territory, **two salespeople call the same prospect** — wasting effort, confusing the customer, and producing an unresolvable argument about whose commission it is. **It is a compensation control as much as a coverage tool.**

**And note the funnel connection:** *lead management* and *opportunity management* are named as one capability because they are **the same object at two stages** — a qualified lead becomes an opportunity, and **the pipeline is just the set of open opportunities weighted by probability of closing.**

items.q: **What are the typical features of a call centre application? How do call centres provide self-service capability, and how do previous call records and the knowledge base help?**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — typical capabilities of call centre applications:**

1. **Predefined escalation route**
2. **Previous records of the caller**
3. **Support in different time zones in different languages**
4. **Managing call assignments**
5. **Knowledge base**
6. **Self service capabilities**
7. **Workflow**
8. **Field service management**

**What the application does:** *"provide customer support by **answering different types of customer queries / calls** and **routing the calls to the most competent person** who can handle it."* Modern call centres support **complex customer interactions — scheduling service requests, providing technical support, and handling financial transactions.**

**Technologies used:** **local area networks (LAN) · automatic call distributors (ACD) · computer technology integration (CTI) · web integration · interactive voice response (IVR) · voice logging and messaging · IVR/speech portals**

---

**The eight capabilities answer four questions about a call, in the order they arise:**

| Question | Capabilities |
|---|---|
| **Who should take this call?** | **ACD**, managing call assignments, **predefined escalation route** |
| **Who is calling, and what happened before?** | **previous records of the caller** — delivered by **CTI** |
| **How does the agent solve it?** | **knowledge base**, **workflow** |
| **Does it need to go further?** | **field service management** — dispatch an engineer |

---

**Previous records of the caller** — the capability the question singles out.

**Without it, every call starts from zero.** The customer re-explains their problem to a third person, and **the company appears not to be one company.** It is **the single customer view arriving in the two seconds before the agent says hello.**

**CTI — Computer Technology Integration — is what delivers it:** it links the telephone system to the customer database so **the screen and the call arrive together.**

**Predefined escalation route** prevents the other classic failure — an agent who cannot solve a problem and does not know who can. **Escalation defined in advance means the path is a rule, not an improvisation.**

---

**The knowledge base and self-service:**

**Once a solution is written down, it can be reused by any agent — and then exposed directly to customers so they never need to call.**

$$\textbf{one agent solves it} \rightarrow \textbf{knowledge base} \rightarrow \textbf{every agent solves it} \rightarrow \textbf{self-service: the customer solves it}$$

**Each arrow removes cost and reduces waiting.** That is the whole economic logic of a modern contact centre.

**And it is the same principle as ESS in HCM and employee e-procurement for indirect items:** *move the transaction to the person who has the need.* **The knowledge base is what makes that transfer possible** — you cannot let customers solve their own problems until the solutions exist in a reusable form.

---

⚠️ **Two capabilities look out of place on a call-centre list and are worth explaining.**

**"Support in different time zones in different languages"** is there because the call centre is often **offshored** — the same **ODC / GDC** model as ERP support in Unit 4, where *support* carried the **highest offshore percentage at 80%** precisely because it is ticket-driven and time-zone difference becomes an advantage.

**"Field service management"** is on the list because **the call is where a service visit is born.** A customer reports a fault by phone; if it cannot be fixed remotely, an engineer must be scheduled. **The call centre and field service are two ends of one process.**

items.q: **What are the typical capabilities of field service applications? What are enterprise marketing management applications? What are the capabilities of PRM, revenue and pricing management, and product configuration applications?**
items.answer:
**Field service applications:**
- **Help in different after-sales service functions — managing installation, service, or repairs of systems or equipment**
- **Support scheduling workforce — which worker should go to which customer site and attend which type of equipment / problem, based on the worker's availability and skill**
- **Managing reverse logistics and spare parts management**
- **Mobile solutions are increasingly an important component**, as companies manage large numbers of **mobile technicians distributed across customer sites**

**Typical capabilities:** **field service management · scheduling workforce · managing spares / service parts · mobile solutions capability**

**Why it is genuinely hard: it is a *constrained assignment* problem.** Every job needs four things to line up:

| Constraint | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Skill** | not every engineer can service every machine |
| **Availability** | they are already booked, or driving |
| **Location** | travel time between sites is real and expensive |
| **Parts** | the right spare must be **on the van**, or the visit is wasted |

> **Any three can be satisfied while the fourth fails — and the visit still achieves nothing.** An engineer with the skill, the time and the location but **not the part** has to come back tomorrow, doubling the cost of the repair.

**That is why "managing spares" sits in a customer-relationship module at all** — it looks like inventory management and is, **but the inventory is distributed across vans**, and the service level it supports is **first-time fix rate**.

**"Reverse logistics" is the distinctive direction:** the faulty part has to come **back** — repaired, refurbished or scrapped. **Service supply chains move goods both ways**, which is why Oracle Inventory Management advertised *"inbound, outbound **and reverse** logistics."*

⚠️ **Mobile is listed as a capability, not a preference, and the reason is structural.** A field engineer is **by definition never at a desk.** If the system can only be updated from an office, either the engineer drives back — losing half a day — or **updates it from memory at the end of the week.**

$$\textbf{no mobile access} \Rightarrow \textbf{data entered late from memory} \Rightarrow \textbf{the single customer view is wrong}$$

---

**Enterprise marketing management applications:**
- **Manage the end-to-end process from gathering and analyzing customer data across web sites and other channels, to planning, budgeting, to executing customer communications and measuring results / effectiveness**
- **Help the enterprise identify and target its best customers and generate qualified leads for the sales team**
- **Encompass capabilities for managing customer loyalty, lists, collateral, and internal marketing resources**
- **Support an integrated approach to marketing strategy, development, delivery and measurement across the marketing mix**

**Capabilities:** **campaign management · customer interaction management · marketing planning · marketing resource and asset management · opportunity / lead management · loyalty marketing**

**The description is a closed loop:**

$$\textbf{gather and analyse} \rightarrow \textbf{plan and budget} \rightarrow \textbf{execute communications} \rightarrow \textbf{measure results} \rightarrow \textit{(back to gather)}$$

**The stage that distinguishes marketing *automation* from marketing is the last one — measurement.** Traditional marketing spend was famously unmeasurable; **running campaigns through a system means response is recorded against the customer record, so effectiveness becomes a number.**

**And note the handoff: *"generate qualified leads for the sales team."*** **Marketing's output is SFA's input** — which is why *opportunity / lead management* appears in **both** lists. **Unqualified leads dumped on a sales team is the classic form of that seam failing.**

⚠️ **Two capabilities are easy to misread.** **"Marketing resource and asset management"** is not about customers at all — it manages **the marketing department's own** budgets, agencies and creative assets. **"Loyalty marketing"** targets **retention** while campaigns target **acquisition** — opposite ends of the funnel, and **the economics favour loyalty**, since retaining an existing customer costs far less than acquiring a new one.

---

**Partner Relationship Management (PRM):**
- **Helps companies manage relationships with different channel partners and thus optimize sales opportunity**
- **Supports partner recruitment and profiling, lead distribution and forecasting, taking partner orders, marketing promotion, partner training, joint business planning, collaborative sales, partner performance management**

**Capabilities:** **partner addition · distributing leads · partner profiling · managing different partner programs · partner opportunity tracking · special partner discounts and approvals · partner service · managing channel inventory / partner pipeline**

**PRM exists because many companies sell *through* dealers, distributors and resellers rather than directly:**

| | **Direct selling (CRM)** | **Channel selling (PRM)** |
|---|---|---|
| Who meets the customer | **your** salesperson | **the partner's** salesperson |
| Who controls them | you — they are employees | **nobody** — the partner is an independent business |
| Who sees the end customer | you | **the partner** |

> **The core difficulty: you cannot instruct a partner, you can only make it attractive for them to sell your product rather than a competitor's.** Every capability is a lever for that — **distributing leads** (you give them business), **special discounts** (margin is the direct incentive), **training and service** (you make it easy to sell yours), **performance management** (you find out which partners deserve more leads).

⚠️ **"Managing channel inventory / partner pipeline" is the most valuable and difficult.** Once goods ship to a distributor you have booked the revenue — but **you no longer know whether they have been sold to an end customer or are sitting in the distributor's warehouse.**

$$\textbf{sold to the channel} \neq \textbf{sold to the customer}$$

**That gap is where the bullwhip effect is born** — and mistaking channel stocking for real demand is how a company keeps producing into a market that has already stopped buying.

---

**Revenue and Pricing Management:**
- **Optimize and manage prices throughout the product life cycle — initial pricing, promotional, and markdown or clearance pricing**
- **Price optimization solutions analyze historical data and incorporate competitive and market information to determine the price sensitivity of a product or a market segment; these models then generate the optimal pricing policy**
- **Price analytics solutions provide price insights that might otherwise be hard to identify**

**Capabilities:** **trade promotion management · promotions · pricing and promotion optimization**

**Pricing is a *life-cycle* decision** — the same product has **three different correct prices at three different moments:**

$$\textbf{initial pricing} \rightarrow \textbf{promotional} \rightarrow \textbf{markdown / clearance}$$

**"Price sensitivity" is the concept underneath it all:** how much does demand fall when price rises? **If demand is insensitive you are leaving money on the table; if it is sensitive, a small cut can pay for itself in volume.** Not knowable by intuition — hence computed from historical and competitive data.

---

**Product Configuration applications:**
- **Help customers configure a product to their desired specification on the web**
- **Based on this configuration, sales staff can quote and generate a price proposal quickly**
- **Automate sales and product configuration, proposal configuration, cost estimation and pricing — compressing the entire lead-to-order process**
- **Popular for complex products and services**

**They solve the *quoting* bottleneck.** For a complex product with thousands of valid combinations, a salesperson historically had to go back to **engineering** to find out whether a configuration was even buildable, then to **finance** for a price — a round trip taking days.

**The application encodes the valid combinations and pricing rules so the answer is immediate — and by putting it on the web, the *customer* can do it themselves.** **It is the configuration counterpart of the e-commerce channel: self-service applied to a task that used to need an expert.**

items.q: **What are the different types of CRM analytics? Give examples of sales, service and marketing analytics.**
items.answer:
**Three types, as the deck defines them:**

**Sales analytics** — *"allows companies to **monitor and understand customer actions and preferences**, through **dashboards that graphically display KPIs**."*

**Marketing analytics** — *"marketing applications generally come with **predictive analytics** to improve **customer segmentation and targeting**, and tools to measure the **effectiveness (ROI) of a marketing / sales promotion campaign**."*

**Customer service analytics** — *"increasing in popularity as companies demand **greater visibility into the performance of call centers and other support channels**, in order to **correct problems before they affect customer satisfaction levels**."*

---

**The three correspond exactly to the three groups of application areas:**

| Analytics | Sits over | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Sales analytics** | SFA, order management, pricing | *what are customers **doing and preferring**?* |
| **Marketing analytics** | campaigns, loyalty, lead management | *who should we **target**, and **did the campaign pay**?* |
| **Service analytics** | call centre, field service | *how is **support performing**?* |

**Each uses a different technique, and the deck names them precisely:**
- Sales analytics uses **dashboards and KPIs** — **descriptive**: *what happened?*
- Marketing analytics uses **predictive analytics** — *what will this segment do?*
- Service analytics is **preventive**: *"correct problems **before** they affect customer satisfaction levels"*

> **Only the marketing one is described as predictive, and that is not accidental.** Marketing must **commit budget in advance of knowing the outcome**, so a prediction has direct value. Sales analytics reports on deals that already exist; service analytics watches a queue that is already forming.

**This is the descriptive-versus-predictive split that the DW-BI chapter formalises:** *"**descriptive** analytics that focuses on history… and **prescriptive** analytics that focuses on trends to predict."*

---

**Examples by type:**

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Sales** | pipeline value and conversion rate by stage · win/loss ratio · revenue per salesperson or territory · **quota attainment** · discount analysis |
| **Marketing** | **campaign ROI** · response rate per channel · **customer segmentation** models · lead-to-opportunity conversion · loyalty programme uptake |
| **Service** | **call volumes and queue lengths** · first-call resolution rate · average handling time · **escalation rate** · SLA adherence · **first-time fix rate** for field service |

---

**How CRM delivers them:** *"CRM applications support different types of customer analytics and reports through **dashboards, built-in reports, custom reports, trend analysis, historical comparison, graphics, drilldown**."*

**Those seven answer questions at three depths:**

| Depth | Capability | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **Glance** | dashboards, graphics | *is anything wrong right now?* |
| **Read** | built-in and custom reports | *what are the numbers?* |
| **Investigate** | trend analysis, historical comparison, **drilldown** | *why, and is it getting worse?* |

**Drilldown matters most and is least visible.** A dashboard showing *"sales down 8%"* is useless alone — the necessary next question is **which region, which product, which salesperson**. **It is exactly the OLAP roll-up / drill-down operation** — *Country → Region → State → City → Sales office* — which is why **CRM analytics is OLAP with a customer dimension**, and why the two chapters sit in the same unit.

⚠️ **Two lines are worth quoting in an answer.** *"Measure the effectiveness (ROI) of a marketing / sales promotion campaign"* — because *half of advertising is wasted and nobody knows which half* is a **measurement** problem, not a spending one. And *"correct problems **before** they affect customer satisfaction levels"* — **by the time satisfaction scores fall, the customers have already left**, so watching queue lengths and resolution times is watching a **leading indicator**.

items.q: **What is PLM? Why is product lifecycle management cross-functional? What are the business drivers for a PLM application?**
items.answer:
> **Source note:** the Unit 5 chapter map lists a PLM chapter, but **no PLM deck was supplied**. This answer is built from the **QnA's own model answer** plus the PLM references inside the other decks — nothing is invented.

**The QnA's model answer:**

- **Product lifecycle management (PLM) is a new set of enterprise applications that manages all data and information about a product from its initial conception to retirement**
- **Product lifecycle includes conceptualization of the product, design, manufacturing, ensuring quality of the product throughout its life cycle, ensuring product safety during its manufacturing, distribution and usage, and finally service — from concept to development till the product retires from service**
- **PLM processes are cross functional — they involve multiple functions: R&D, Engineering, Marketing, Production, Quality, Sales and Service**

---

**Why it is cross-functional** — the answer is contained in the span itself. **No single department owns a product for its whole life:**

| Function | What it does to the product |
|---|---|
| **R&D** | conceives it |
| **Engineering** | designs it |
| **Production** | makes it |
| **Quality** | certifies it |
| **Marketing** | positions it |
| **Sales** | sells it |
| **Service** | repairs it |

$$\textbf{one product} \times \textbf{seven functions} \Rightarrow \textbf{seven partial views, unless something unifies them}$$

> **That is the information-silo problem for a third time** — the same defect as Nestlé's twenty-nine vanilla records and as the fragmented customer view CRM exists to fix.

**The most useful framing for an answer is the parallel with the other two modules:**

| Module | Manages the life cycle of | From | To |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HCM** | **an employee** | recruitment | retirement |
| **CRM** | **a customer** | lead | repeat customer |
| **PLM** | **a product** | **initial conception** | **retirement from service** |

**All three are the same architectural idea: take one long-lived entity and hold every piece of information about it in one place, across every function that touches it.** That is why *"Hire-to-Retire"* and *"concept to retirement"* sound alike.

---

**Business drivers for a PLM application** — verbatim from the QnA:

1. **Product Variants and growing product lines**
2. **Shorter product development cycles**
3. **Cost reduction pressure**
4. **Reduced engineering resources**
5. **Collaboration needs with local and global partners**
6. **Regulatory compliance pressure**
7. **Process and data integration needs between R&D, Production, Supply**
8. **Innovation focus — business model, processes, product**
9. **Intellectual asset management**
10. **Documentation control**

*(The printed list repeats "product variants and growing product lines" at both ends — treat it as **ten distinct drivers**, not eleven.)*

**They fall into four groups, which is how to reproduce them under exam conditions:**

| Group | Drivers | The pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **More products, less time, less money** | product variants and growing lines · shorter development cycles · cost reduction pressure · reduced engineering resources | **do more with less, faster** |
| **More people involved** | collaboration with local and global partners · integration between R&D, Production, Supply | **designed across organisations** |
| **More rules to obey** | regulatory compliance pressure | **safety and environmental law** |
| **More to protect and record** | intellectual asset management · documentation control · innovation focus | **the design *is* the asset** |

**The first group is a squeeze from both ends and is the strongest single argument for PLM.** Companies produce **more variants of more products in less time with fewer engineers** — and **those four cannot all be satisfied by working harder.** The only way is to **stop re-designing what has already been designed**, which requires knowing what exists.

**The second group explains why it must be a system rather than a shared drive.** When *"hundreds of sub-part suppliers"* co-develop a product — the phrase is from this unit's own collaborative-planning slide — **design data crosses company boundaries**, and email cannot manage revision control across organisations.

**The third group is where PLM becomes non-optional.** Regulatory compliance is not a benefit you choose; **you cannot sell a chemical, a drug or a vehicle without the documentation.** The question bank's PLM items dwell on exactly this — **environmental safety, product compliance, chemical safety, hazardous material management, regulatory reporting, and the master safety data sheet.**

**And documentation control is the mechanism underneath all of it.** A product's specification changes hundreds of times; **knowing which revision is current, and which revision a shipped unit was built to, is the difference between a targeted recall and a total one.**

---

**PLM's three current capability areas**, from Unit 3's evolution table: **earlier = Quality Mgmt, Product Development Project mgmt → now = Product Data Management · Document Management · Product Safety.**

**And the clearest concrete contribution — the EBOM/MBOM distinction from Unit 4:**

| | **EBOM** | **MBOM** |
|---|---|---|
| Built by | **engineering** | **manufacturing** |
| Structured by | **function** — how the product works | **assembly sequence** — how it gets built |
| Includes | designed components | **plus packaging, consumables and anything the factory needs that the engineer never listed** |

**EBOM ≠ MBOM, and reconciling them is a real problem in practice.**

> **That handover is also the honest answer to "how does a PLM application differ from an ERP application?" — PLM manages the product *before and around* it is made; ERP manages *making and selling* it.** PLM's world is designs, revisions, documents and approvals; ERP's is orders, stock, costs and postings. **The BOM is where they meet**, and the same physical part carries **one identity in design and another in production**.

**Market:** the assignment names two leading vendors — **SAP (SAP PLM)** and **PTC (Windchill)**.

items.q: **What is supply chain management? What flows does it track, and what is the SCOR model?**
items.answer:
**Definition:**
- **SCM is the oversight of materials, information, and finances as they move in a process from supplier to manufacturer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer**
- **Supply chain management involves coordinating and integrating these flows both within and among companies / users**
- **Goal of an effective supply chain management system is to reduce cost of inventory and efficient movement of materials (supply)**

**A fuller definition the deck also gives:** *"SCM is the management of a network of interconnected activities towards the provision of product and/or service packages required by the end customers. **Since customers may have customers (B2B) in turn, this forms a business chain or supply chain.** SCM spans all movement and storage of raw materials, work-in-process inventory, and finished goods from point of origin to point of consumption."*

> **The phrase *"both within and among companies"* is what separates SCM from everything before it in this course.**

**ERP optimises inside one company. SCM optimises across companies that do not share a management, a system or an incentive** — a fundamentally harder problem, because **you cannot instruct your supplier the way you can instruct your own plant.**

$$\textbf{MRP: one factory} \rightarrow \textbf{MRP II: one company} \rightarrow \textbf{ERP: one enterprise} \rightarrow \textbf{SCM: the network}$$

**That is Unit 3's four-decade evolution table with its last ring named.**

**Why SCM became crucial:** **manufacturing at multiple sites, many vendors, distributors** — *"consider the situation of **Big Bazaar** ordering for supply of plastic chairs to a manufacturer with many facilities across the country"* — and it is **a method to optimize overall demand and supply flow**. *(The deck also calls it **IRP — Intelligent Resource Planning**, a deck-specific label.)*

**SCM typically includes:** **inventory management** *(track costs and needs, optimize levels)* · **warehouse management** *(space utilization, interfaces to material moving equipment, material identification technology)* · **transportation management** *(carrier selection, loading, routing, scheduling)*.

**And current-day SCMs support "open data models"**, allowing data sharing **outside the enterprise**: **suppliers know inventory status; customers know order status and lead times.** ⚠️ **That is the technical precondition for everything else in the chapter** — VMI, CPFR and collaborative forecasting are all applications of it. *(A classical ERP is **closed by design**; SCM requires the opposite.)*

---

**The three flows:**

| Flow | Contents | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Material movement** | **movement of goods from a supplier to a customer** | **downstream** |
| **Information / documentation** | **mandatory forms, import/export, licence-permit**; *"transmitting orders and updating the status of delivery"* | **both ways** — orders up, status down |
| **Financial tracking** | **payment schedules, COD (Cash on Delivery) handling** | **upstream** |

$$\textbf{goods flow down} \qquad \textbf{money flows up} \qquad \textbf{information flows both ways}$$

> **The information flow is the one that can be improved almost for free, and that is the whole leverage of modern SCM.** Moving material faster costs money — faster trucks, more warehouses. **Moving information faster costs almost nothing once systems are connected — and better information substitutes directly for inventory.**

**That substitution is the chapter's recurring theme:** **VMI** replaces buffer stock with **shared consumption data**; **CPFR** replaces two conflicting forecasts with **one shared forecast**; **cross-docking** replaces storage with **synchronised schedules**. **Every one trades inventory for information.**

---

**The SCOR model — SCOR = Supply Chain Operational Reference:**

$$\textbf{Plan} \cdot \textbf{Source} \cdot \textbf{Make} \cdot \textbf{Deliver} \cdot \textbf{Return}$$

**The diagram draws them repeating along the chain:**

$$\textbf{Suppliers' Supplier} \rightarrow \textbf{Supplier} \rightarrow \textbf{Your Company} \rightarrow \textbf{Customer} \rightarrow \textbf{Customer's Customer}$$

with each link carrying **Source · Make · Deliver** and **Return** beneath, and **Plan** sitting above — the company's own Plan spanning the whole chain.

**Three features carry the meaning:**

**① The same five processes repeat at every link.** **Your *Deliver* is your customer's *Source*.** That is what makes it a **reference** model — **one vocabulary that describes every company in the chain**, so two trading partners can talk about their processes in the same terms. *(It is Unit 4's "your goods issue is your customer's goods receipt", generalised to five processes and five companies.)*

**② Plan sits above the others and spans further.** Each company plans its own link, but **your Plan reaches across suppliers and customers** — the diagram's way of saying that **planning is where cross-company coordination happens.** **Source, Make, Deliver and Return are executed locally; Plan is what has to be shared.** That split is precisely the **SCP-versus-SCE** distinction.

**③ Return is a first-class process, not an afterthought.** Most process models stop at Deliver. **SCOR gives returns equal standing because reverse logistics is a real and expensive flow** — recalls, warranty, faulty goods, end-of-life.

**The deck's own aside — *"Have we seen this slide earlier? — BPM!"*** — points at Unit 2: **SCOR is one of the named process-modelling standards**, alongside **APQC, BPMN, EPC and UML**. **It is a business process framework that happens to be about supply chains.**

---

**The seven "rights" of logistics — deliver:** the right **product · quantity · condition · place · time · customer · price**. *"These seven rights highlighted the importance of moving and storing materials in an efficient, timely, and reliable manner."*

**They are not seven independent goals — they are seven ways one delivery can be wrong**, and getting six of seven right still means the delivery failed.

**Related terms:** **WIP · ASN (Advanced Shipping Notice) · GRN (Goods Received Note) · AWB / Bill of Lading · VMI · 3PL (Third Party Logistics)**

⚠️ **And the deck's motivating question is its thesis in disguise:** *"consider the cost of a mineral water bottle — how much at the corner shop? how much would be the raw material cost? Is there a difference?"* **The water is nearly free; almost the entire retail price is bottling, packaging, transport, storage and margin.**

$$\textbf{retail price} - \textbf{raw material cost} = \textbf{the supply chain}$$

**Which is why supply chain optimisation is worth so much for low-value, high-volume goods — and why retail is named as the industry with the highest reliance on it.**

items.q: **What is strategic, tactical and operational planning? Give examples of each. How do they differ by criticality and time horizon? Discuss the evolution of supply chain planning software.**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — supply chain planning helps decisions at 3 levels:**

**1) Strategic decisions: Long term decisions**
- **Critical decision for the company having long term implications — # years** *(even beyond the annual business plan)*
- **Factory geography, warehouse locations, sources for procurement — local / global, etc.**
- **Decisions are difficult to reverse without substantial cost for the change**
- **These decisions influence the company's long term profit and sales goal**

**2) Tactical decisions: Medium term decisions**
- **Applicable for months to quarters**
- **Sales and Operations planning, MPS, MRP fall in this category**

**3) Operational decisions: Short term decisions**
- **Reviewed week / daily**
- **Vendor schedules, distribution plan, transportation and route plan fall in this category**

---

**The deck's diagram — "different planning horizons need separate SCP" — spans Years → Minutes and gives each level a question and its tools:**

| Level | Cadence | **The question** | **Planning tools** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strategic** | **Yearly / Quarterly** | *"What is my long term capacity management strategy? What is my most optimized **network design**?"* | **Network Design · Long Term Planning (LTP)** |
| **Tactical** | **Monthly / Weekly** | *"How do I meet my monthly customer requirements?"* | **S&OP · MPS · MRP** |
| **Operational** | **Daily / Hourly** | *"How do I schedule my orders, my transport routes?"* | **Detailed scheduling · Transportation Planning · Route scheduling** |

---

**How they differ by criticality — the key insight is *reversibility*, not merely time.**

The QnA gives it away for the strategic level: *"decisions are **difficult to reverse without substantial cost** for the change."*

| Level | Decision | Cost of changing your mind |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategic** | **build a factory in Pune** | **enormous** — land, plant and people are committed |
| **Tactical** | **produce 8,000 units next month** | **moderate** — adjust the schedule, absorb some inventory |
| **Operational** | **send truck 4 via this route** | **negligible** — reroute it |

> **Time horizon and reversibility go together for a physical reason: the longer the horizon, the more concrete the commitment.** A factory is bricks; a route is a line on a map.

**That is why the three need "separate SCP" tools rather than one system with a date filter.** A network-design tool answers *where should things be* over years, evaluating land costs, subsidies and transport lanes. A route optimiser answers *which way should this truck go this afternoon*. **Same company, completely different mathematics.**

**And on impact:** *"strategic supply chain decisions have **maximum impact** on business."* The chart plots **ROI / Impact** against **Planning Horizon**, and the reason is that **strategic decisions set the constraints every lower decision must work inside:**

$$\textbf{network design} \Rightarrow \textbf{which lanes exist} \Rightarrow \textbf{what routes can be optimised}$$

**No amount of brilliant route optimisation recovers the cost of a warehouse in the wrong city.**

⚠️ **Two notes on the chart deserve mention.** The deck flags that ***"time axis direction is reverse to usual"*** — years on the left, hours on the right, so that impact **falls** as you move rightward. **Reading it without noticing the reversal inverts the conclusion.** And it notes the ***"overlaps in the 3 plans"*** — the boundaries are gradients, exactly as Unit 3 said of MRP II's five levels: *"there will be gaps between each planning level and also with execution levels."*

⚠️ **Note also that the tactical level is the entire MRP II ladder from Unit 3.**

$$\textbf{Tactical} = \textbf{S\&OP} + \textbf{MPS} + \textbf{MRP}$$

**Everything Unit 3 spent five topics on sits inside *one* of SCM's three levels** — which is the implicit argument for why SCP exists. **MRP II has no strategic level at all** (its top is the Business Plan, a target rather than a network design), and its operational level stops at PAC inside one factory. **SCP adds a level above MRP II and extends the level below it across companies.**

**Industry segments with high reliance on supply chain:** **retail · distributed manufacturing businesses.** **Retail leads because almost its entire cost structure is supply chain** — there is no manufacturing efficiency to find, so **logistics *is* the business.**

---

**The evolution of supply chain planning software** — the deck plots **richness of functionality** against **value perception** across three generations:

| Generation | Capabilities |
|---|---|
| **MRP II** | **Material Requirement Calculation · Calculation of Machine/Labour Resource · Sales & Ops Plan (SOP) · Master Schedule (MPS) · Order Promising (ATP) · Distribution Plan (DRP) · Capacity Planning** |
| **ERP** | **all of MRP II** + **Demand Planning** + **Integration with SCM execution systems** *(Transport, Warehouse, Materials Management, Production Execution)* |
| **SCM Planning & Collaboration** | **Advanced Demand Planning · Supply Chain Planning and Optimization · Production scheduling, Optimization · Transportation Planning, Route Optimization · Global Available to Promise · Advanced Collaboration (VMI, CPFR)** |

*("Term SCM became popular post 1995.")*

**The ladder is cumulative, and each rung adds one word to the rung below it:**

| Rung | What it added |
|---|---|
| **MRP II** | **calculation** — work out material and capacity requirements |
| **ERP** | **integration** — connect planning to the execution systems that carry it out |
| **SCM** | **optimization** and **collaboration** — find the *best* plan, and make it *jointly* |

**Compare the same capability at two rungs and the pattern is unmistakable:**

| MRP II / ERP | SCM |
|---|---|
| Demand Planning | **Advanced** Demand Planning |
| Order Promising (ATP) | **Global** Available to Promise |
| Distribution Plan (DRP) | Transportation Planning, **Route Optimization** |
| Capacity Planning | Production scheduling, **Optimization** |

> **Every SCM entry is an ERP entry with "advanced", "global" or "optimization" attached** — precisely the *transaction → decision* movement Unit 3's *earlier-vs-now* tables described. **And it is why the two products overlap and co-exist rather than one replacing the other.**

**The deck's own note says it plainly:** *"while ERP evolved to become more comprehensive in functionality, **niche applications like SCP focused on key areas and specialized**… so **ERP and SCP may co-exist, overlapping at times**. **DRP of the traditional ERP has quickly grown to become an application by itself.**"*

**DRP is the clearest instance:** in Unit 3 it was one slide inside production planning; **here it has become Transportation Planning with Route Optimization, a product category with its own vendors. A feature became an application.**

items.q: **Discuss the difference between supply chain planning and execution. What types of processes are included in each? Explain the difference between ERP and supply chain planning software.**
items.answer:
**The three terms first:**
- **SCM is sometimes broken down into the stages of planning, execution and shipping**
- **Supply Chain Planning (SCP) and Supply Chain Execution (SCE) are the two main categories of SCM**
- **SCP is the component of supply chain management involved with predicting future requirements to balance supply and demand**

> **SCP's definition is worth reading slowly: *"predicting future requirements to **balance supply and demand**."*** That is the same sentence as S&OP's purpose in Unit 3 and as capacity planning's *"A is not directly linked to B, hence a mismatch"*. **Balancing supply against demand is the single problem this course keeps returning to, at successively wider scopes** — one work centre, one factory, one company, one distribution network, and finally **the whole chain**.

---

**Supply Chain Planning vs Supply Chain Execution:**

| | **Supply Chain Planning** | **Supply Chain Execution** |
|---|---|---|
| **Processes** | **Network Design · Demand Planning · Supply Planning · Material Planning · Sales and Operations Planning · Safety stock planning · Inventory Planning · Production Planning · Detailed Scheduling · Distribution planning · Transportation Planning · Vehicle Scheduling · Route Planning** | **Inventory Management · Procurement · Vendor Management · Warehousing · Sales Order Management · Production Order Mgmt · Shipping · Transport Execution · Quality Management** |
| **Applications** | **ERP, Supply Chain Planning solutions** | **ERP** |
| **Vendors** | **SCP solutions (SAP APO, i2 Technologies, Oracle APS)** · **ERPs (SAP, Oracle)** | **SAP ERP · Oracle ERP · Other ERPs** |

**The distinguishing test is simple: *does anything physically happen?***

| | **Planning** | **Execution** |
|---|---|---|
| Produces | **a plan** — numbers about the future | **a transaction** — a record that something happened |
| Can be re-run | **yes, freely** — simulate as often as you like | **no** — a posted goods receipt is a fact |
| Needs | optimisation algorithms | **authorisation, workflow, audit trail** |

**The deck's own note names exactly that difference:** *"planning software need not worry about aspects such as **access control, transaction management, workflow execution**. These are the must / should features of execution software such as ERP."*

> **That is why the Applications row is asymmetric, and it is the most examinable cell in the table:**

$$\textbf{Planning: ERP } \textit{or} \textbf{ SCP solutions} \qquad\qquad \textbf{Execution: ERP } \textit{only}$$

**Specialist planners exist; specialist executors do not.** You can buy a better optimiser than your ERP's, because **optimisation is a self-contained mathematical problem.** You cannot easily buy a better transaction processor, because **execution must post to the ledger, respect authorisations and leave an audit trail** — all of which live in the ERP.

**Same level-dependent conclusion as Unit 4's inventory pyramid:** *the lower the level, the stronger the case for integrated ERP; the higher the level, the stronger the case for best-of-breed.*

⚠️ **Some process pairs appear on both sides with different verbs, and telling them apart is what the question is testing:**

| Planning | Execution |
|---|---|
| **Transportation Planning · Vehicle Scheduling · Route Planning** | **Transport Execution · Shipping** |
| **Inventory Planning · Safety stock planning** | **Inventory Management** |
| **Production Planning · Detailed Scheduling** | **Production Order Mgmt** |
| **Material Planning** | **Procurement · Vendor Management** |

**The deck admits the boundary is soft:** *"both planning and execution activities are different and distinct, **but the boundaries are blurred** — for example transportation planning and shipping."* **The reliable discriminator: planning decides *what should happen*; execution records *what did*.**

**A worked SCE example the deck gives, in retail:** goods receipt, goods issue, inventory management, and merchandise distribution via warehouse and transport management. **Each nests further** — *goods issue* → **creating outbound delivery, pick, pack, final goods issue**; *creating outbound delivery* → **vehicle scheduling, route determination, staging area and picking location determination, planning for proof of delivery**; *posting goods receipt* → **posting GR, quality check, invoice verification, final settlement.** **One line item expands into five real decisions per shipment — which is what "transaction intensive" means concretely.**

---

**ERP versus Supply Chain Planning — the nine-row comparison:**

| | **ERP** | **Supply Chain Planning** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | **Transaction and Basic Planning** | **Advanced Planning and Optimization** |
| **Planning Order** | **Sequential planning of material and capacity** | **Simultaneous planning of material and capacity** |
| **Prioritization Handling** | **Cannot handle any prioritization rule** | **Can handle any prioritization rules (Customer, Product etc.)** |
| **Simulation** | **Limited simulation capability** | **Extensive simulation capability** |
| **Constraints planning** | **Cannot do any constraints based planning** | **Can do constraint based planning** |
| **Capacity Mgmt** | **Plan based on infinite capacity** | **Can plan based on finite capacity** |
| **Forecasting** | **Basic forecasting capability** | **Advanced — statistical forecasts / causal models** |
| **Replanning** | **Replanning takes long time** | **Replanning can be very quick** |
| **ATP** | **Limited order promising capability** | **Advanced — alternate location or alternate product** |

> **Every row of that table is one of MRP's seven limitations from Unit 3, answered.** Laying them side by side is the strongest possible answer:

| MRP limitation (Unit 3) | SCP row that answers it |
|---|---|
| *"cannot consider **actual capacity**… assumes capacity is infinite"* | **finite capacity planning** |
| *"cannot consider **constraints** and vendor's limitations"* | **constraint based planning** |
| *"**cannot do any optimization**"* | **Advanced Planning and Optimization** |
| *"**cannot replan fast enough**"* | **replanning can be very quick** |

**Four of the seven, matched one-for-one** — not a coincidence. **SCP is the product category that exists because MRP has those limitations**, exactly as Unit 3 said of APS.

**Two rows are worth understanding rather than memorising:**

**① Sequential vs simultaneous planning.** MRP plans **material first**, then checks capacity afterwards — which is why **closed-loop MRP** has to loop back to MPS when the check fails. **SCP plans material and capacity together in one pass**, so the plan it produces is feasible when it emerges. **The loop disappears because the constraint was inside the calculation from the start.**

**② Global ATP.** ERP's ATP answers *"do we have it, here, on that date?"* — a lookup. **SCP's answer is a search**: if not here, **another location**; if not this product, **an alternate product**; if nothing exists, **can we make it in time (capable-to-promise)?** **That is why it needs finite-capacity data to answer at all.**

**The deck's own summary is the fairest one-line verdict:** *"in a nutshell, **SCP has advanced functionality over ERP; but ERP has higher integration and execution capability**. Of course, these differences are at some point — over time product vendors, both ERP and SCP, bridge these gaps based on market forces."*

items.q: **What is network design? What decisions are taken during it, when do companies look for a network design solution, and how do such solutions identify optimum locations? What are the typical capabilities of a supply chain planning tool and how do demand planning capabilities differ between ERP and SCP?**
items.answer:
**The eight SCP modules first:** **network design · demand planning · supply network planning · production planning · detailed scheduling · transportation planning · vehicle scheduling · route planning**

**They are the three planning levels in order** — **one strategic** (network design), **three tactical** (demand, supply network, production planning), **four operational** (detailed scheduling, transportation, vehicle scheduling, route planning). **The granularity gets finer and the module count rises as the horizon shortens**, exactly as in MRP II's five levels.

---

**Network Design — objective:** *"designing the supply chain network — i.e. **locating the factories, warehouses and distribution centers in the most optimal location** that reduces overall supply chain cost and provides needed customer service."* **It is a *strategic* planning activity.**

**Typical network design decisions:**
- **Where new locations (Plants, Warehouses, DCs, Stores) shall be opened?**
- **Which products shall be produced at which locations?**
- **Which customers should be assigned to which distribution centers?**
- **What are the capacity requirements for plants / distribution centers?**
- **Which locations shall be closed?**

**They split into two kinds, and noticing that is the answer to "what types of decisions":**

| Kind | Decisions |
|---|---|
| **Where things are** | **where to open · which locations to close · capacity requirements** |
| **How the network is used** | **which products at which locations · which customers to which DCs** |

> **The second kind is the surprising and valuable half.** Even with the network fixed, **assigning products to plants and customers to distribution centres is itself an optimisation** — and it can be changed **without building anything**, which makes it the cheapest lever on the list.

**"Which locations shall be closed?" is the decision companies avoid and the model does not.** Closing a plant is politically and humanly hard, and an optimiser recommends it dispassionately — **which is why the cost list explicitly includes "costs for opening / closure of locations."**

---

**When companies look for a network design solution:**
- **A company wants to expand its activities to another country**
- **Change in product demand over time — locations might become unprofitable, so some may have to shut down and new ones open**
- **Introduction of a new product — where to produce, how to distribute**

> *"So **SCP is not a one-time static exercise**. It can be used regularly, since business will keep facing the above events regularly."*

**How optimum locations are identified — the cost considerations:**
- **Transportation costs · Production costs · Storage costs · Handling costs · Procurement costs · Penalty costs for delayed or non-fulfilled demand**
- **Location-related Fixed operating costs · Costs for opening / closure of locations · Government subsidies for location**

*(The deck's note adds more: **strategic impact on business, export/import special zones, storage safety, local labour laws, infrastructure availability.**)*

**They divide into three families:**

| Family | Costs |
|---|---|
| **Flow costs** *(scale with volume)* | transportation · production · storage · handling · procurement |
| **Location costs** *(scale with sites)* | fixed operating · opening / closure |
| **Distortions** | **penalty costs for delayed or non-fulfilled demand** · **government subsidies** |

⚠️ **The two distortions are the interesting ones.** **Penalty costs are how service level enters a cost model** — without them, the cheapest network is one warehouse serving the world very slowly. **Subsidies are how policy enters.**

**Network Design Vendors: ILOG Logic Tools · i2 Supply Chain Strategist.**

---

**The service-versus-cost trade-off** — the deck's worked figures *(Fig. 25.6, p. 384)*:

| | **Optimal Network For Cost** | **Optimal Network For Service** |
|---|---|---|
| **Savings** | **\$6 million** | **\$3 million** |
| **Service** | **40% next day** | **80% next day** |

$$\textbf{Doubling next-day service } (40\% \rightarrow 80\%) \textbf{ costs } \$3\text{m of the }\$6\text{m saving}$$

> **There is no "right" answer between the two networks, and that is the lesson.** The cost-optimal network **consolidates into few large facilities**; the service-optimal network **spreads into many local ones**. **Consolidation is cheap and slow; dispersion is fast and expensive.**

**This is the same trade-off as DRP's competing objectives in Unit 3** — *"providing finished products at the correct location"* versus *"minimize finished goods inventory in the network"* — and as **Level vs Chase**, and as **service-level-based inventory** in Unit 4. **Four appearances of one structure.**

**What the optimiser actually provides is not the answer but the *curve*:** for each level of service, the cheapest network that achieves it. **Choosing a point on that curve is a business decision** — and the deck's note says so: *"cost optimization is key; **but weighed against risks**. So a variety of what-if situations have to be allowed."* **Which is exactly what "simulation capability" means in the ERP-versus-SCP table.**

---

**Supply Network Planning Tool Capabilities:** **feasible plan considering constraints · medium term planning with day bucket · critical component planning · prioritization · simultaneous planning · simulation · collaborative planning · detailed distribution planning and Transport Load Building · different planning approaches**

**Two phrases carry most of the weight.** **"Medium term planning with day bucket"** names both horizon and granularity — **medium term** places it tactical, **day bucket** means per-day rather than per-week. **Finer buckets mean a more actionable plan and a much larger computation.** And **"critical component planning"** answers a real problem: a product may have thousands of components but **only a handful are genuinely scarce** — **planning everything at maximum detail is wasteful; planning the constraints at maximum detail is what determines the outcome.** *(That is Rough Cut Capacity Planning's logic applied to materials: optimise the bottleneck, approximate the rest.)*

---

**Demand planning capabilities:** **forecasting at different planning levels · consistent planning · forecasting for quantity or value · data visibility as per planning need · statistical forecasting · forecasting based on a number of parameters · consensus forecasting · collaborative forecasting · planning for promotion · planning for new products · planning for discontinuation / phase out · macros**

**ERP vs SCM demand planning:**

| **ERP Tool** | **SCM Tool** |
|---|---|
| **Some simple statistical forecasting tools** | **Extensive statistical capability, large number of forecasting tools** |
| **Does not support causal / multi-variate models** | **Supports causal / multi-variate models** |
| **Does not support like modelling** | **Supports like modelling** |
| **No advanced promotion planning** | **Supports advanced promotion planning** |
| **No collaborative forecasting** | **Supports collaborative forecasting** |
| **Very little exception handling** | **Advanced macros, alerts, automated e-mail for exceptions** |
| **Basic drill down** | **Better drill down and graphical capability** |
| **Data not stored in a data warehouse** *(SAP ERP uses LIS-based info structures)* | **Historical data stored in a data warehouse — larger volumes, better performance** |

**Three rows name techniques rather than adjectives and deserve unpacking:**

**① Causal / multi-variate models.** A simple statistical forecast extrapolates **the product's own history**; a **causal model** uses *other* variables — **price, weather, competitor activity, economic indicators, promotions.**

$$\textbf{time-series: } y_t = f(y_{t-1}, y_{t-2}, \dots) \qquad \textbf{causal: } y_t = f(\text{price}, \text{weather}, \text{promotion}, \dots)$$

**The difference bites whenever the future is not like the past — which is exactly when a forecast matters most.**

**② Like modelling** forecasts a product **with no history** by borrowing the history of a similar one. **A new phone model has no sales history; the previous model does.** **This is what makes "planning for new products" possible at all.**

**③ Consensus vs collaborative forecasting** are different, and the pairing is deliberate: **consensus** reconciles sales, marketing, finance and production numbers **inside one company** *(S&OP's arbitration made into software)*; **collaborative** reconciles your forecast with your **customer's**, **across companies** *(and becomes CPFR)*.

⚠️ **"Planning for Discontinuation / Phase out" is the capability people forget**, and it is symmetric with new products. A product being phased out has **falling demand for a knowable reason** — and a forecast that extrapolates its history will **over-order right up to the end**, leaving exactly the obsolete stock that the *inventory obsolescence* KPI measures and that *heavy markdown* eventually clears. **Launch and phase-out are the two moments when history is the worst possible guide.**

**And the last row is why the DW-BI chapter is in the same unit:** an SCM tool stores forecast history **in a data warehouse** while ERP stores it in operational structures. **That is not a storage detail — it is why one can hold years of history and analyse it quickly and the other cannot.**

items.q: **Explain the capabilities of production planning and detailed scheduling tools, of the GATP module, and of transportation planning and optimisation tools. What business problems do they solve?**
items.answer:
**Production Planning and Detailed Scheduling — typical capabilities:**
- **Up to the minute production schedule and material requirement planning**
- **Simultaneous quantity and capacity requirement planning**
- **Multi-level material and capacity availability check capability**
- **Optimization capability for set-up optimization and sequence optimization**
- **Automatic replanning in case there is any change in requirement — replanning is very fast**
- **Simulation and what-if capability**
- **Can create automatic exception messages**

**These tools plan at a much more detailed level, considering everyday factory constraints — machine breakdown, delay in supply from a particular supplier, change in customer order — detailed up to the minute with specific start and end time for each operation.** *"By optimizing order sequences, these tools help in **reducing lead times, reduce stocks and at the same time improve on-time delivery performance**."*

**Approaches supported: heuristics based planning · optimization algorithms · bottleneck scheduling**

**Leading vendors: SAP APO Production Planning – Detailed Scheduling · i2 Factory planner**

---

**"Set-up optimization and sequence optimization" is the capability that most clearly does something MRP cannot.**

On many machines, **the time to change over between jobs depends on what ran before.** A paint line changing from **white to black is quick; black to white requires a deep clean.**

$$\textbf{same jobs, different sequence} \Rightarrow \textbf{different total setup time} \Rightarrow \textbf{different capacity available}$$

> **MRP cannot see this at all** — it schedules by due date and treats setup as a fixed number. **A scheduler that sequences light-to-dark creates capacity out of nothing but ordering.**

**Which is why the stated benefits are three at once — *reduced lead times, reduced stocks, improved on-time delivery*.** Normally those trade against each other; **better sequencing improves all three simultaneously because it removes waste rather than reallocating it.**

**The three approaches are three answers to an intractable problem:**

| Approach | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Heuristics** | apply sensible rules — *earliest due date first*, *shortest job first*. **Fast, good enough, no guarantee** |
| **Optimization algorithms** | search for the mathematically best sequence. **Better result, much more computation** |
| **Bottleneck scheduling** | **schedule the constraint resource first** and fit everything else around it |

**Bottleneck scheduling is the most practical** and rests on one observation: **the bottleneck determines the plant's output, so an hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost by the whole factory, while an hour lost anywhere else costs nothing.**

⚠️ **"Automatic replanning… replanning is very fast" answers MRP's limitation ⑤.** If replanning takes overnight, **the shop floor spends the day executing a plan that is already wrong.** And **that speed is what makes simulation possible at all** — *a what-if that takes eight hours is not a what-if, it is a project.* **The two capabilities are the same capability.**

---

**Global Available-To-Promise (GATP):**

**ATP is "an online search to verify the company's ability to provide the requested product, in the requested quantity, and on the date requested by the customer"** — but in ERP it is **"limited, based on static info."**

**Supply chain solutions provide advanced capabilities:**
1. **Alternate products**
2. **Alternate location**
3. **Multi-site multi-product availability check**
4. **Multi-level component and capacity check (Capable to promise)**
5. **Rule based availability check**
6. **Calendars**

**The six are an escalating sequence of answers to one customer question — *"can I have it by Friday?"***

| If… | GATP tries |
|---|---|
| it is not in **this** warehouse | **alternate location** — check the others |
| **this exact product** is unavailable | **alternate products** — a substitute the customer would accept |
| **nothing finished** exists anywhere | **capable-to-promise** — can we *make* it in time? |
| the answer depends on **who is asking** | **rule based availability check** |
| the date depends on **working days and shifts** | **calendars** |

**The distinction to state explicitly:**

$$\textbf{ATP: is there stock or a planned receipt?} \qquad \textbf{CTP: could we produce it, given components and capacity?}$$

**CTP requires exactly what SCP has and ERP lacks — finite capacity and multi-level component visibility.** That is why the deck calls it *"multi-level component **and capacity** check."* **You cannot promise to make something without knowing whether the machine is free.**

**"Rule based availability check" is the commercially interesting one.** When stock is short, **who gets it?** A rule can reserve stock for **strategic customers** or allocate by **contract commitment**, rather than serving whoever ordered first. **First-come-first-served is a policy, not a law of nature** — and this is the same **prioritization** capability the ERP-vs-SCP table said ERP *"cannot handle."*

**The deck's note:** *"with only ERP, advanced ATP can be achieved to some degree **with manual analysis**."*

---

**Transportation planning and optimisation — the three areas:**

| **Technology Used** | **Business Need** | **What it does** |
|---|---|---|
| **Transport planning and Vehicle scheduling** | **Minimize number of vehicles used** | **when and what size vehicle needs to be ordered**, looking at the daily shipment plan, service level required and vehicle capacity |
| **Route optimization** | **Minimize vehicle travel distance** | **build an optimum route keeping multiple drop points in mind**, so trucks travel the shortest route while dropping at all points |
| **Optimum truck load building** | **Minimize unloading labour, and also so the truck does not run empty** | **build an optimum load** — takes account of **drop sequence** and **material properties** *(light materials should not be below heavy material)* |

**Transport Optimizer Constraints:** **vehicle capacity · depot location · limits of distance, duration, stopovers · handling resources · maximum storage time at location · vehicle types (trains, ships, aircraft, trucks) · opening hours of locations · drop sequence · stacking constraint · access restriction**

*(The deck's note adds: **border crossings allowed only at certain times of day, governmental quota restrictions, material-related constraints — perishable, hazardous**, and that stacking constraints alone are a long list — *this side up, hazardous, LIFO, interchange with another vehicle*. **Most long-distance transportation happens through containers.**)*

**The three areas minimise three different things, and they interact:**

$$\textbf{how many vehicles} \qquad \textbf{how far each travels} \qquad \textbf{how well each is packed}$$

> **Load building and route optimisation are coupled through drop sequence, and that coupling is the elegant part.** The load must be packed so that **each drop's goods are reachable when the truck arrives** — which means **the last delivery is loaded first, deepest in the truck.** **You cannot decide the packing until you know the route, and the route affects how much fits.**

**And the physical constraint on top of it — *"light materials should not be below heavy material"* — is a genuine safety and damage rule the software must respect.**

**This is why the deck says *"route optimization is one of the most complex problems in computer science."*** It is the **vehicle routing problem**, a generalisation of the travelling salesman problem — and adding capacity, time windows, stacking rules and access restrictions makes it dramatically harder.

⚠️ **The best single illustration of why shortest-path alone is insufficient:** *"access restriction could be something related to **border crossing**, which is allowed only at certain times of the day."* **The shortest route may be unusable at the hour the truck arrives — so the optimiser is scheduling in time, not just routing in space.**

**Other asides worth carrying:** **optimizations based on seasons** *(the deck's "case of Finland customer")* · **route operation permits** for **special item movement and long structures** · and *"even **airlines** use some of these techniques while connecting multi-hop, multi-segment travel itineraries"* — **the same mathematics, different vehicles.**

items.q: **What is VMI? Explain the VMI process. What are the advantages and disadvantages of VMI? Explain collaborative forecasting, collaborative product development and collaborative replenishment, and how collaborative solutions evolved.**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — VMI:**

- **VMI is a process where the supplier makes inventory replenishment decisions for the customer**
- **Vendor monitors the buyer's inventory levels and makes decisions as to which items to send, how much quantity and when**
- **Customer sends demand and inventory information on a prearranged schedule, typically daily / weekly**
- **In VMI, the customer does not generate a P.O. — instead the supplier drives replenishment of products and creates the order**
- **Customer sends inventory, daily sales data (in retail this can be POS data) and promotion information to the supplier via EDI message**
- **Supplier's fulfilment system does the order processing — including invoicing**
- **Payment is made with an electronic fund transfer from the customer's bank**

**History:** **VMI was popularized in the late 1980s by Wal-Mart and Procter & Gamble.** *"The success of Procter and Gamble's program with Wal-Mart helped VMI to become a globally accepted replenishment practice."*

---

**The VMI process**, as the deck's diagram draws it:

**Customer side** sends, by EDI: **daily stock data from the inventory system · daily sales data (past sales) · planned future promotions**

**Supplier side** then: builds a **Sales Forecast** → **Decides Replenishment of Inventory** → **Determines Replenishment Quantity** *(considering **Transport Load Quantity**)* → **generates a CRP order and sends it to the retailer via EDI**

**Customer** then: **reviews the order and, if required, makes changes** → sends an **EDI Order Acknowledgement**

**Supplier** then: **processes the order and sends an Advance Shipping Notification (ASN)** → **Customer receives the ASN and prepares for receipt of material**

*(**EDI = Electronic Data Interchange**, *"a standard of communication for business and trade; there are specific standards such as **EDIFACT**"*. **Vendor = Supplier.**)*

---

> **The single most examinable sentence is *"the customer does not generate a P.O."*** — because it inverts the entire procurement cycle from Unit 4.

| | **Normal procurement** | **VMI** |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides what to order | **the customer** | **the supplier** |
| Who raises the order | **customer** → PO | **supplier** → CRP order |
| Direction of the trigger | customer **pulls** | supplier **pushes**, informed by consumption |
| What the customer sends | **a purchase order** | **stock, sales and promotion data** |

**Everything Unit 4's procurement chapter described — requirement determination, source determination, order processing — is done by the *vendor*.** The customer's remaining role is **to send data and to review.**

**Why this is better rather than merely different:** the supplier now sees **actual consumption** rather than **a filtered order signal**. In normal procurement, the retailer's ordering pattern is the *only* thing the supplier can see — and **that pattern is distorted by the retailer's own batching, safety stock and lot sizing.** **VMI removes the distortion by sharing the underlying data**, which is exactly why *"eliminating bullwhip effect"* is the first benefit.

**Note the *"review the order, if required make changes"* step** — VMI is not blind, **the customer retains a veto**, which is what makes it acceptable. And **payment by electronic fund transfer without an invoice-driven cycle is essentially ERS from Unit 4** — the supplier's system invoices itself, because both parties already agree on quantity and price.

---

**Benefits of VMI:**
1. **Eliminating Bullwhip effect — less variability**
2. **Uniform production for supplier**
3. **Lower administration cost**
4. **Lower transportation costs**
5. **Lower inventories**
6. **Increased sales and service**
7. **Suppliers know real market demand information**

**Difficulties faced in VMI:**
- **Unstable pricing environment / sudden surge in demand are difficult to handle**
- **VMI requires a critical volume of business (% of supply)**

> **The seven benefits are not independent — six follow from the seventh, and showing that chain is what earns marks:**

$$\textbf{suppliers know real market demand} \Rightarrow \textbf{less variability} \Rightarrow \textbf{uniform production} \Rightarrow \textbf{lower inventories and transport costs}$$

*("Lower administration cost" comes from a different cause — **no PO, no invoice matching, no order chasing**; "increased sales and service" from better availability.)*

**The two difficulties are equally worth understanding:**

**① Unstable pricing / sudden demand surge.** VMI works by **extrapolating consumption**. A price change or spike **breaks the extrapolation** — and because the customer is no longer ordering, **there is no signal to say the world changed** except the data itself, arriving after the fact. *(Which is exactly why **planned future promotions** is one of the three EDI feeds — the mechanism for warning the supplier about a deliberate spike.)*

**② Critical volume of business.** Setting up VMI costs both parties real integration effort. **A supplier providing 2% of your purchases cannot justify it, and neither can you** — **the saving is proportional to volume while the setup cost is fixed.** ⚠️ **That threshold is why VMI is a Wal-Mart-and-P&G story rather than a universal practice**, and why supplier collaboration sits at **levels 2 and 3 of the procurement maturity model** rather than level 1.

---

**The three kinds of collaborative planning:**

**Collaborative forecasting** — *"a customer company in the supply chain can provide useful forecast / demand input to the supplier company."* Example: *"a **tyre manufacturer** can have an idea of the number of vehicles planned for the next quarter by its customer companies."*

**Collaborative replenishment** — *"replenishment orders can be picked up / sensed by supplier companies, being part of an intelligent supply chain."* Also **rate contracts**; and **see VMI**.

**Collaborative product development** — *"when complex products are produced — especially new models — **hundreds of sub-part suppliers** involved will have to closely co-operate based on status of completion across the supply chain."*

**They share information at three different points in time:**

| Kind | Shares | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Collaborative forecasting** | **what we expect to need** | **before** anything is ordered |
| **Collaborative replenishment** | **what we are actually consuming** | **as** it happens |
