| **Collaborative product development** | **what we are designing** | **before the product exists** |

> **The tyre example makes the forecasting case unanswerable.** A tyre manufacturer's demand is **completely determined by its customers' vehicle production plans** — it is **dependent demand across a company boundary.** Forecasting it statistically from tyre sales history is **guessing at something that is already known, by someone else.**

**That is the deep point: collaboration converts an independent-demand problem into a dependent-demand one.** Unit 3 drew that line at the company's edge; **collaboration moves the line outward.**

---

**How collaborative solutions evolved — five stages:**
1. **Customers interacted through hard copy documents**
2. **Customers expose material requirement to suppliers through portals**
3. **Suppliers expose to customers next delivery schedule etc.**
4. **Sharing of [goods accepted — payment status], electronically**
5. **VMI & collaborative forecasting**

**And the evolution chart plots *collaboration / trust* against time:**

$$\textbf{Paper based updates} \rightarrow \textbf{Portals} \rightarrow \textbf{Collaborative Forecasting, VMI} \rightarrow \textbf{CPFR}$$

> **The vertical axis being *trust* is the whole explanation.** Each stage requires the parties to reveal more — and at stage 5, **the supplier sees your inventory and daily sales, from which they can infer your margins, your promotions and your relationships with their competitors.**

**Technology was never the constraint** — EDI existed for decades. **Trust was.** The deck's note is unusually reflective: *"many of these may look trivial in the current age of on-line access, SMS alerts etc. **But it was a big deal not too long ago.** Also, businesses won't embrace technology so quickly."*

⚠️ **Note the direction of stage 3.** Stages 2, 4 and 5 are the **customer** revealing things; stage 3 is the **supplier** revealing their delivery schedule. **Collaboration has to be reciprocal or it is just surveillance** — and the deck is candid that in practice it is often asymmetric: *"at times **customer businesses force the supplier** to adopt automated collaboration channels."*

items.q: **What is CPFR? How did it evolve? Explain the nine steps of the CPFR process. What is the bullwhip effect and how do these techniques address it?**
items.answer:
**CPFR — Collaborative Planning, Forecasting and Replenishment:**

- **CPFR started as a vision for some of the large retailers like Wal-Mart in the 1990s, who found the biggest problem of supply chain is that the company and their supplier do not work with the same forecast numbers and execute replenishment using this**
- **Collaboration between company and supplier is key for effective forecasting and replenishment planning**

**CPFR Process:**
- **Customers and suppliers submit their own individual forecasts**
- **These are combined into one shared, agreed-upon forecast**
- **Joint forecast is done through sharing — sales data, existing inventory, and stock-out information, promotions, and supplier production constraints**

---

**The diagnosis is the whole idea:** *"the company and their supplier **do not work with the same forecast numbers**."*

**Both parties forecast the same future demand and get different answers, because each sees only part of the picture:**

| Party | Sees | Cannot see |
|---|---|---|
| **Retailer** | **actual sales**, planned promotions, store-level stock | the supplier's **production constraints** |
| **Supplier** | **their own capacity**, other customers, material lead times | **actual end-consumer demand** |

**So they plan against each other.** The retailer plans a promotion the supplier cannot supply; the supplier builds capacity for a volume that never comes. **Neither is wrong from where they stand — the information is split.**

$$\textbf{two forecasts} \Rightarrow \textbf{two plans} \Rightarrow \textbf{one of them is wrong, and both parties pay}$$

> **CPFR's answer is not a better forecasting algorithm — it is a *single* forecast.** And the four things shared are exactly the four things each party was missing: **sales data and stock-out information** and **promotions** (retailer → supplier), and **production constraints** (supplier → retailer).

**VMI and CPFR compared:**

| | **VMI** | **CPFR** |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides | **the supplier alone** | **both, jointly** |
| Shared | consumption data | **the forecast itself, plus a joint business plan** |
| Scope | **replenishment** | **planning, forecasting and replenishment** |
| Formality | a practice | a **standard** — the VICS nine-step framework |

**VMI delegates; CPFR agrees.** That is why CPFR sits **above** VMI on the collaboration evolution chart — it needs more trust and covers more.

---

**The nine steps of CPFR** — **VICS (Voluntary Intra Industry Commerce Standards) created a standard: a 9-step reference framework for collaboration and performance tracking:**

1. **Develop Collaboration Arrangement**
2. **Create Joint Business Plan**
3. **Create Sales Forecast**
4. **Identify Exceptions to Sales Forecast**
5. **Resolve Exceptions to Sales Forecast**
6. **Create Order Forecast**
7. **Identify Exceptions to Order Forecast**
8. **Resolve Exceptions to Order Forecast**
9. **Generate Order**

**They group into four phases** *(the deck's diagram marks them P · C · R · F)*:

| Phase | Steps | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan** | **1–2** | develop collaboration arrangement · create joint business plan |
| **Forecast (sales)** | **3–5** | create · identify exceptions · resolve exceptions |
| **Forecast (order)** | **6–8** | create · identify exceptions · resolve exceptions |
| **Replenish** | **9** | generate order |

> ### **Agree, then forecast twice, then order.**

**Steps 3–5 and 6–8 are the *same three steps* applied to two different forecasts** — which is why nine steps are much easier to remember than they look.

**The distinction between the two forecasts is the examinable part:**

$$\textbf{Sales forecast} = \text{what the end consumer will buy}$$
$$\textbf{Order forecast} = \text{what the retailer will order from the supplier}$$

**They are not the same number.** Sales forecast is **consumer demand**; order forecast is that demand **adjusted for the retailer's own inventory position, lot sizes, promotions and store openings.** A retailer might sell 1,000 units a week and order 4,000 once a month — **the sales forecast is smooth, the order forecast is lumpy.** **And that gap is precisely where the bullwhip effect is born**, which is why CPFR forecasts both explicitly.

⚠️ **The exception-handling steps (4, 5, 7, 8) are four of the nine — nearly half — and skipping them is the standard mistake.**

**The point of a joint forecast is not that the two parties always agree; it is that *disagreement is detected and resolved before it becomes two different plans*.** An **exception** is a divergence beyond an agreed tolerance — *your forecast says 1,200, mine says 800.*

> **Without steps 4–5 and 7–8, CPFR would just be two forecasts exchanged by email. The exception process is what makes it a single forecast.**

**Same discipline as exception messages in MRP** — *"getting values that are outside the expected range… prioritize the messages → take action"* — applied across a company boundary. **And step 1 comes before everything for a reason:** *"develop collaboration arrangement"* is where the parties agree **what will be shared, how often, in what format, and what tolerance counts as an exception.** **Without that agreement, step 4 has no definition of "exception" to work with.**

---

**The bullwhip effect** — the deck charts it as four panels moving upstream:

$$\textbf{Consumer Sales} \rightarrow \textbf{Retailer's Order to Wholesaler} \rightarrow \textbf{Wholesaler's Order to Manufacturer} \rightarrow \textbf{Manufacturer's Order to Supplier}$$

**showing the same underlying demand with progressively larger swings.** *(The deck's note: "this is a characterization of a real-world phenomenon.")*

**Consumer sales are relatively smooth. Each link upstream adds variability for reasons that are individually rational:**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Order batching** | the retailer sells 100/day but orders **500 once a week** — a smooth demand becomes a spiky order |
| **Safety stock adjustment** | demand rises 10%, so the retailer orders 10% more **plus** more safety stock — **amplifying the increase** |
| **Lead-time reaction** | long lead times mean each link over-orders to cover uncertainty |
| **Promotions and forward buying** | a discount causes a large one-off order that does not reflect consumption |
| **Shortage gaming** | expecting rationing, buyers **over-order deliberately** |

$$\textbf{small change in consumer demand} \xrightarrow{\text{each link amplifies}} \textbf{large swing at the manufacturer}$$

**The manufacturer at the far end sees violent swings caused by a market that barely moved** — and responds by building capacity and stock for peaks that are artefacts.

> **Every cause has the same root: each link can only see the orders from the link immediately below it, not actual consumption.**

**Which is exactly why VMI eliminates it** — the supplier receives **POS data and stock levels, not orders**, so **the distorting filter is removed.** **And it is why CPFR exists too:** a **shared forecast** means the manufacturer is not inferring demand from an order pattern at all.

**Both techniques attack the bullwhip by replacing an order signal with a data signal.**

---

**SCM vendors, for completeness:** **i2 / JDA** *(strong in Retail)* · **SAP APO** · **Oracle APS / Value Chain Planning** · **Manugistics / JDA** · **Adexa** · **Demantra** · **Logility** · **Aspentech** *(strong in Process Industry)* · **IFS** · **IBM's ILOG SCO**

⚠️ **The list quietly documents heavy consolidation** — *"being 'smaller' compared to ERP systems, there is **more churn by way of mergers/acquisitions**. **JDA has acquired quite a few companies.**"* **Both "i2 / JDA" and "Manugistics / JDA" appear on one list** — two once-independent vendors, both now JDA. **That is the financial-viability criterion demonstrated inside a single slide**, and why *"ERP vendors claim advantage of integration to ERP."*

items.q: **Define a data warehouse. What are its characteristics? Discuss its advantages and disadvantages, its typical capabilities, and its three-tier architecture.**
items.answer:
**Definition:**

> **A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile collection of data used in support of the management decision making process.**

**And the working description:** *"a data warehouse **sources data from various operational systems, organizes and stores it** in a form that is **standardized, structured, consistent, clean and integrated** — structured in a way to specifically address the **reporting and analytic requirements**."*

---

**The four characteristics:**

| Characteristic | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Subject-oriented** | **organized around subjects such as sales, product and customer**; focuses on **modeling and analysis of data for decision makers** |
| **Integrated** | **constructed by integrating multiple heterogeneous sources** — OLTP, ERP, CRM, legacy applications |
| **Time-variant** | **provides information from a historical perspective** — e.g. **past 5–10 years** |
| **Non-volatile** | **data once recorded cannot be updated — cannot be changed until the next refresh** |

**Mnemonic: SITN — and each characteristic is a deliberate *rejection* of how an operational system works:**

| Characteristic | Operational system | Data warehouse |
|---|---|---|
| **Subject-oriented** | organised by **process** — order entry, goods receipt | organised by **subject** |
| **Integrated** | **one application's** data | **many sources**, reconciled |
| **Time-variant** | **current** state only | **5–10 years** of history |
| **Non-volatile** | **updated constantly** | **write once, read many** |

> **Every one is the opposite of an OLTP design, and that is the point — you cannot build good analytics on a database optimised for transactions.**

**"Non-volatile" is the least intuitive and the most important.** An operational system **overwrites**: change a customer's address and the old one is gone. **A warehouse never overwrites** — otherwise **last year's report would silently change every time someone corrected a record today, and no analysis would ever be reproducible.**

**The warehouse is further characterized by:** **it is for strategic decision making · the data is integrated · it contains historical data over a long time horizon · it is oriented around various subjects · it is mainly read-only with periodic batch updates from operational sources.**

**And structurally:** *"the data warehouse contains data with **several levels of detail: current detail data, old detail data, lightly summarized data and highly summarized data**"*, it is **optimized for read-only transactions**, and **the applications that run on it include OLAP, data mining tools and query tools.**

⚠️ **"Several levels of detail" is examinable in its own right.** A warehouse holds **the same facts at four granularities simultaneously** — because a dashboard asking *"total sales by region this year"* should not scan a billion transactions to produce one number, **while detail must remain available for drill-down.** **Holding both levels is how you refuse to choose.**

---

**The three-tier architecture:**

$$\textbf{Data Sources} \rightarrow \textbf{Data Migration (ETL and Data Loading Tools)} \rightarrow \textbf{Data Storage Repository} \rightarrow \textbf{Data Analysis: Reporting, OLAP, Data Mining}$$

**The deck's diagram shows it concretely:** **CRM · Billing · ERP · Flat Files · Other Data Sources → ETL → Data Warehouse → Reporting · Analytics · Data Mining** — with the fuller version adding **Data Marts** and **OLAP Servers (MOLAP, ROLAP)** between the warehouse and the analysis tools, and **External Sources** and **Operational Database** as the sources.

**The architecture is the four characteristics turned into boxes**, and tracing that correspondence is the strongest way to answer:

| Characteristic | Which part of the architecture delivers it |
|---|---|
| **Integrated** | **the ETL layer** — reconciling CRM, billing, ERP and flat files |
| **Subject-oriented** | **the warehouse schema** — star schemas organised by subject |
| **Time-variant** | **the warehouse itself** — accumulating loads over years |
| **Non-volatile** | **the load process** — periodic batch, never transactional update |

**The ETL layer is the load-bearing one, and that is why it gets its own tier.** Bringing CRM, ERP and legacy data together means resolving **different customer IDs, different date formats, different units, different definitions of "revenue"** — which is **Nestlé's twenty-nine vanilla records arriving in the analytics layer.**

**Separating the tiers buys three things:**
- **Analytical load never touches production systems** — a heavy query cannot slow down order entry *(the deck names this outright as an advantage: **"better performance of source system"**)*
- **Sources can change without breaking reports**, because only the ETL layer knows their formats
- **One warehouse serves many analysis tools** — OLAP, query/reporting and data mining all read the same repository

---

**Data warehousing capabilities:** **data storage · database integration · supporting different data types · application and middleware integration · software platform integration · security features** *(authentication, authorization, access control, permission management, encryption, monitoring/alerting/auditing)* **· high availability and reliability** *(redundancy, fault tolerance, replication and mirroring, backup, recovery, disaster recovery)* **· supporting industry standards** *(SQL, SOA — web services, XML)* **· administration features** *(system monitoring, diagnostics, job scheduling)* **· metadata management, data modeling, hierarchy management**

**Notice how much of that list is *not* about analysis** — security, high availability, backup, administration, standards. **Only the last line is analytical.**

> **The reason: a data warehouse becomes a critical system.** Once management decisions run on it, **it must be as available and as protected as the transaction systems that feed it** — and it now contains **the entire company's data in one place**, which makes it a far more attractive target than any single source system.

**Metadata management is the most under-appreciated item.** Metadata is **data about the data** — where a figure came from, how it was calculated, when it was refreshed. **Without it, two reports showing different revenue numbers cannot be reconciled, and users stop trusting the warehouse. A warehouse nobody trusts is worse than no warehouse, because it still costs money.** *(And **hierarchy management** is what makes drill-down work at all.)*

---

**Advantages and disadvantages:**

| **Pros** | **Cons** |
|---|---|
| **Common Data Model** | **Data latency** |
| **Clean Data** | **Unstructured data reporting not possible** |
| **Better performance of source system** | |
| **Facilitate reporting** | |

*(The topic summary adds **"storage of data for longer period"** as an advantage.)*

⚠️ **Both disadvantages follow directly from characteristics you were just told were advantages — and saying so is the mark-earning observation.**

**① Data latency is the price of non-volatility.** Because the warehouse is loaded by **periodic batch** rather than updated transactionally, **it is always out of date by one refresh cycle.**

$$\textbf{non-volatile + batch load} \Rightarrow \textbf{latency}$$

**Which is why an ODS exists** — *"an ODS consolidates data from multiple source systems and provides a **near real time** integrated view of current data."* **The ODS is the answer to this specific disadvantage.**

**② Unstructured data is excluded by the schema.** A warehouse stores facts and dimensions in tables. **Emails, documents, images, call recordings and social media posts do not fit** — and they are exactly the data the CRM chapter said could be valuable *("from outside the organization if needed, like social media")*.

**And "better performance of source system" is the advantage people forget** — it benefits the *operational* systems, not the analysts. **Moving reporting off OLTP is often the original business case, before anyone has run a single analysis.**

items.q: **Explain a star schema. Define fact and dimension table. What are its advantages? Discuss data granularity, refreshing, quality data properties, and ETL tools.**
items.answer:
**The star schema:**
- **The classic star schema is a frequently used multi-dimensional model for relational databases**
- **It classifies two groups of data: facts (sales or quantity, for example) and dimension attributes (customer, material, time, for example)**
- **It uses fact and dimension tables and is composed of a single fact table and, for each dimension, one dimension table**
- **Fact tables are related to each dimension table in a Many-to-One relationship (Primary / Foreign Key Relationships)**

**Fact** — **numeric measurements (values) that represent a specific business aspect or activity**, stored in a **fact table at the center of the star schema**, containing facts **linked through their dimensions**. *Typical example: individual sales records.*

**Dimensions** — **qualifying characteristics that provide additional perspectives to a given fact**, stored in **dimension tables**, **joined to the fact table by a foreign key**. *Typical examples: time periods, geographic region (markets, cities), products, customers, salesperson.*

**Attributes** — **provide additional information for a dimension.** *For example customer name, city and region can be attributes for the dimension Customer.*

**Advantages of the star schema:**
- **Storing data in the form of the classic star schema is optimized for reporting**
- **It allows the user to view facts from a variety of perspectives (dimensions)**

---

**The deck's worked example** *(an image-only slide, so easy to miss):*

**Fact table — SALES:** **Product_Code · Period_Code · Store_Code · Units_Sold · Dollars_Sold · Dollars_Cost**

| Dimension table | Columns |
|---|---|
| **PRODUCT** | **Product_Code** *(key)* · Description · Color · Size |
| **PERIOD** | **Period_Code** *(key)* · Year · Quarter · Month · Day |
| **STORE** | **Store_Code** *(key)* · Store_Name · City · Telephone · Manager |

**Look at the SALES table and the structure gives itself away — it has exactly two kinds of column:**

| Kind | Columns | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Foreign keys** | Product_Code, Period_Code, Store_Code | **the dimensions** — *what, when, where* |
| **Measures** | Units_Sold, Dollars_Sold, Dollars_Cost | **the facts** — the numbers |

$$\textbf{fact table} = \textbf{keys pointing outward} + \textbf{numbers to add up}$$

**That is the whole design, and why it is called a *star*** — one central table with dimension tables radiating from it, joined many-to-one.

**The test for "is this a fact or a dimension":**
- **Facts are things you would *add up*** — units sold, dollars sold, cost
- **Dimensions are things you would *group by* or *filter on*** — product, month, store

**"Total Dollars_Sold, by Month, for Blue products, in Mumbai stores"** uses one fact and three dimensions — **that single sentence is what the schema is built to answer.**

**Note the dimension → attributes hierarchy:** the **PERIOD** dimension carries **Year, Quarter, Month, Day** — **those attributes *are* the drill-down path.** **Attributes are not decoration; they are the axes along which you roll up and drill down.**

**And notice what STORE contains that a fact table never would — Store_Name, Telephone, Manager.** Descriptive, textual, unaggregatable. **Putting them in the dimension keeps the fact table narrow, and a narrow fact table is a fast one when it holds a billion rows.**

⚠️ **The star schema is *deliberately denormalised*, and this is the point most often got wrong.**

| | **OLTP — normalized** | **Warehouse — star schema** |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | **avoid update anomalies** | **avoid joins** |
| Because | data changes constantly | **data is non-volatile — it does not change** |
| Cost | many joins per query | some storage redundancy |

> **The justification is non-volatility.** Normalisation exists to prevent inconsistency **when data is updated — and warehouse data is not updated.** **So the reason for normalising evaporates, and you may trade storage for query speed freely.**

---

**Data granularity — the trade-off:**

**Summarized level:** **reduced storage costs and reduced CPU usage · increased performance since fewer records to process · better reporting performance.** **But: summarized data cannot answer transaction level questions.**

**Detailed level:** **each transaction's details can be obtained. But the problem is volume of data — too voluminous.**

$$\textbf{summarized: fast, cheap, cannot drill down} \longleftrightarrow \textbf{detailed: slow, expensive, answers anything}$$

**The practical resolution is not to choose** — it is to hold **both**, which is why a warehouse contains *"current detail, old detail, lightly summarized and highly summarized"* data.

> **The unrecoverable direction is what makes this decision matter: you can always summarise detail; you can never recover detail from a summary.** So the risk is asymmetric — over-summarise and the question you cannot answer next year is **permanently unanswerable**.

---

**Refreshing the warehouse:**

**Options:** **periodically** *(every night, every week)* · **after every significant event** *(say after each month-end financial closing)* · **on every update** *(as soon as data changes)*
**Techniques:** **full refresh from base tables** · **incremental or delta refresh**

| Option | Freshness | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Periodically** | up to a day/week stale | **low** — runs overnight when systems are quiet |
| **After significant events** | aligned to **business meaning** | low, and **consistent** |
| **On every update** | **near real time** | **high** — constant load on OLTP |

**"After every significant event" is the subtle one:** refreshing after **month-end closing** means the warehouse always holds *closed, reconciled* figures — **never a half-closed month that would produce misleading reports.** **Business meaning, not clock time, defines the boundary.**

**And the two techniques differ enormously in cost:** **full refresh** is simple, safe and **completely impractical once the warehouse is large**; **delta refresh** loads only what changed — far cheaper, **but it requires knowing what changed**, i.e. a change-capture mechanism in the source system.

---

**Properties of Quality Data:** **Accuracy · Completeness · Integrate · Timeliness · Consistency and Standardization · Accuracy of Hierarchical relationships · Uniqueness**

**Three of the seven bite hardest in an ERP context:**

**① Uniqueness** — **one real-world thing must be one record.** This is **Nestlé's twenty-nine vanilla records** stated as a data-quality property, and it is hardest when integrating multiple sources: *"Ramesh Kumar"* in CRM and *"R. Kumar"* in ERP are the same customer.

**② Consistency and standardization** — **the same thing must be recorded the same way everywhere.** Different date formats, units, currency conventions. **This is what the "T" in ETL spends most of its time on.**

**③ Accuracy of hierarchical relationships** — **the drill-down paths must be correct.** If a city is assigned to the wrong region, **every regional report is wrong and every drill-down leads to the wrong place** — and **the error is invisible at the summary level**, which is what makes it dangerous.

> **This whole list is "garbage in, garbage out" from Unit 1 given seven names** — and why *clean data* is both an advantage of warehousing and a named ERP success factor. **The warehouse does not create quality; the ETL layer has to impose it.**

---

**ETL tools — the QnA's model answer:**

**"ETL tools enable companies to extract data from multiple sources (Extract), reformat and cleanse it (Transform), and load (Load) it into another database, a data mart or a data warehouse for analysis."**

| Step | Capability |
|---|---|
| **Extract** | **batch extraction of high volumes of data from one or more sources** |
| **Transform** | **after extraction, the data needs to be transformed or modified depending on specific business logic, so that it can be sent to the target repository** |
| **Load** | **loading of data to specified target systems** — data warehouse, data mart, ODS, another application |

**Areas of usage:** **data migrations · master data management · data warehousing and reporting · compliance**

**ETL vendors come from three backgrounds:** **pure-play** *(Ascential Software — DataStage; Informatica — PowerCenter)* · **database vendors** *(IBM; Microsoft, Pervasive; Oracle Warehouse Builder)* · **BI vendors** *(Business Objects, Cognos, Hummingbird, SAS)*

> **"Transform" is the step doing the real work — it is where the four data-warehouse characteristics are actually manufactured:**

| Transform does | Delivering |
|---|---|
| reconciling customer IDs across systems | **Integrated · Uniqueness** |
| standardising formats, units, currencies | **Consistency and Standardization** |
| restructuring process data into subjects | **Subject-oriented** |
| stamping records with a load date | **Time-variant** |

**Extract and Load are plumbing; Transform is where the data warehouse's promises are kept.**

**And only one of the four usage areas is analytics.** **"Data migrations" is the connection back to Unit 4** — the ERP project's master and transaction data migration objects have to move from legacy to new system, and **ETL is the tool that does it**; *"validation of data before loading"* was a named core-team responsibility. **"Compliance" is the least obvious** — regulators require reports drawing on several systems, and **ETL assembles them repeatably and auditably**, which links to **SOX compliance** in Unit 3's finance evolution row.

items.q: **Explain OLAP and OLTP processing. What are the characteristics of each and how are they different? What analysis options and functionalities does OLAP provide, and what are the three types of OLAP?**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer:**

**OLTP (Online Transaction Processing):**
- **OLTP refers to a class of systems that facilitate and manage transaction-oriented applications, typically for data entry and retrieval**

**Characteristics:**
1. **OLTP manages ongoing transactional data related to business operations like production, sales data etc.**
2. **OLTP is the source of the data origin. Every data of the business is stored in the OLTP system**
3. **OLTP database design is highly normalized in nature**
4. **Follows Entity Relationship diagram and uses data modeling**
5. **Involves relational database management system (RDBMS)**

**OLAP (Online Analytic Processing):**
- **OLAP enables a user to easily and selectively extract and view data from different points-of-view. OLAP data is stored in a multidimensional database, providing rapid access to data for analysis. OLAP is part of the broader category of business intelligence and data mining tools**

**Characteristics:**
1. **Data is consolidated for a period of time**
2. **OLAP database is formed from various databases which are OLTP in nature**
3. **OLAP provides decision making information and does analysis**
4. **Database design is typically denormalized with limited tables**
5. **The data reveals multi-dimensional views of various kinds of business activities**

---

**The differences table:**

| **OLTP System** | **OLAP System** |
|---|---|
| **Holds current data** | **Holds historical data** |
| **Stores detailed data** | **Can store both detailed and highly summarized data** |
| **Data is dynamic — changes with every transaction** | **Data is largely static** |
| **Transaction driven** | **Analysis driven** |
| **Supports day-to-day transactions / decisions** | **Supports strategic decisions** |
| **A large number of operational users** | **Low number of managerial users** |
| **High number of transactions** | **Medium to low level of transactions** |

> **The whole table follows from one difference in workload, and deriving it is much stronger than reciting it:**

$$\textbf{OLTP: many users, tiny operations, constant writes} \qquad \textbf{OLAP: few users, huge queries, rare writes}$$

| Because the workload is… | The design must be… |
|---|---|
| **many small writes** (OLTP) | **normalized** — avoid update anomalies, keep writes cheap |
| **few enormous reads** (OLAP) | **denormalized** — avoid joins, keep reads fast |
| **current state matters** (OLTP) | **overwrite** — no need to keep history |
| **trends matter** (OLAP) | **accumulate** — history *is* the data |

**This is the same reasoning as the star schema's denormalisation, restated at the system level: normalisation protects writes; denormalisation accelerates reads.**

**The two rows about users are the ones people skip and the most telling** — *"a large number of operational users"* versus *"low number of managerial users"*: **thousands of clerks entering orders, versus a few dozen managers asking questions.** **That difference alone justifies separate systems**, and is why *"better performance of source system"* is an advantage of warehousing.

⚠️ **And OLAP characteristic ② states the dependency:** *"OLAP database is formed from various databases which are OLTP in nature."* **OLAP has no data of its own.** OLTP is *"the source of the data origin"*; **OLAP is downstream, always — which is why data latency is unavoidable.**

---

**Types of analysis possible in OLAP:** **aggregation · comparison · ranking**

**OLAP functionalities:** **roll up and roll down (drill-up and drill-down) · slice and dice · multidimensional data cube · pivot · sort**

**Strengths of an OLAP tool:** **powerful visualization tool · provides fast, interactive response times · good for analyzing time series · can be useful to find some clusters and outliers**

**The five functionalities are five ways to move through a cube:**

| Operation | What it does | On the deck's CPG cube |
|---|---|---|
| **Roll up** | **aggregate to a higher level** | City → State → Region |
| **Drill down** | **the reverse — expose detail** | Region → State → City |
| **Slice** | **fix ONE dimension**, view the rest | *"the **Food** slice"* — Product = Food |
| **Dice** | **fix a range on SEVERAL dimensions** | Food and Personal care, in APAC and Europe, Retail only |
| **Pivot** | **rotate — swap which dimension is on which axis** | Products-as-rows becomes Regions-as-rows |

**Slice vs dice is the distinction most often examined and most often confused:**

$$\textbf{Slice: one dimension fixed to one value} \qquad \textbf{Dice: several dimensions restricted to sub-ranges}$$

> **A slice cuts one flat plane out of the cube; a dice cuts a smaller cube out of the cube.**

**The deck's worked examples are worth reproducing.** The **roll-up/drill-down hierarchy** is **Country (India) → Region (West) → State (Maharashtra) → City (Mumbai) → Sales office** — with the fuller version showing **East Zone / West Zone → Gujarat, Maharashtra, Assam, Bengal → Mumbai, Pune, Kolkata → Nariman Point, Vikroli.** The **CPG cube** is **Product** *(detergent, food, personal care, healthcare)* × **Sales Channel** *(retail, wholesale, export)* × **Regions** *(APAC, Americas, Europe)*, and the **multidimensional data cube** example is **Time Period (1Qtr–4Qtr) × Product (TV, VCR, PC) × Country (India, China, Mexico, Australia)** with **sum** along the edges.

**Roll-up and drill-down are what make the hierarchy in the dimension tables useful** — the **PERIOD** dimension's *Year, Quarter, Month, Day* attributes **are the rungs you roll up and down.** **This is the same drill-down capability listed under CRM analytics — CRM analytics is OLAP over a customer dimension.**

**And the three analysis types map onto the operations neatly:** **aggregation** is roll-up, **comparison** is what pivot and dice are for, and **ranking** is sort applied to an aggregate.

---

**The three types of OLAP** differ in **where the data physically lives**, and the middle letter gives it away:

| Type | Storage | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **ROLAP** — **Relational** OLAP | data stays in **relational tables**; cubes computed on the fly | **scales to huge volumes**; **slower** queries |
| **MOLAP** — **Multidimensional** OLAP | data **pre-aggregated into a multidimensional cube** | **very fast**; **limited size**, long load times |
| **HOLAP** — **Hybrid** OLAP | **summaries in a cube, detail left relational** | fast at summary level, **drills through to detail** |

> **HOLAP is the granularity trade-off implemented as an architecture** — *"reduced storage costs and better reporting performance"* from the summarised side, *"each transaction's details can be obtained"* from the detailed side, **both at once.**

**Note that MOLAP and ROLAP are named in the architecture diagram as the two OLAP *server* types** feeding the analysis tools — **they sit between the warehouse and the user**, which is why they are called *servers*: **the warehouse stores; the OLAP server presents.**

**And "good for analyzing time series" is not a throwaway strength.** Time is present in nearly every cube, and it has a **natural hierarchy** (day → month → quarter → year) with **natural comparisons** (this month vs last month vs same month last year). **OLAP is built for exactly that shape of question — which is what the Time-variant characteristic exists to support.**

items.q: **What is a data mart and how does it differ from a data warehouse? What is an ODS and how does it compare? What is data mining, what are its uses and steps, and what cautions apply? What is analytics and how does it differ from business intelligence?**
items.answer:
**Data mart:** **a subset of a data warehouse that supports the requirements of a particular department or business function.**

**Characteristics:** **small · flexible · lightly summarized · departmentally structured**

**Differences from a data warehouse:**
- **A data mart focuses on only the requirements of users associated with one department or business function**
- **Data marts do not normally contain detailed operational data, unlike a data warehouse**
- **As data marts contain less data, they can be more easily navigated**

**Advantages of a data mart:**
1. **To give users access to the data they need to analyze most often**
2. **To provide data in a form that matches the needs of users in a department or business function**
3. **To improve end-user response time due to the reduction in the volume of data to be accessed**
4. **Normally use less data, so cleansing, loading, transformation and integration are far easier — hence implementing a data mart is simpler than establishing a corporate data warehouse**
5. **The cost of implementing data marts is normally less than establishing a data warehouse**

**The five advantages reduce to two:**

| Advantage | Reduces to |
|---|---|
| 1, 2 — the data they need, in their form | **relevance** |
| 3, 4, 5 — faster, simpler, cheaper | **size** |

**And the relationship the deck states is the important one:** *"a data warehouse can source data from different data sources and, **in turn, is a source of data for several data marts**."*

$$\textbf{many sources} \rightarrow \textbf{one warehouse} \rightarrow \textbf{many data marts}$$

> **The warehouse fans data in; the marts fan it back out — which matters because the integration happens ONCE, centrally.** The marketing mart and the finance mart are **guaranteed to agree**, because both descend from the same reconciled warehouse.

⚠️ **Building marts *directly* from source systems is the failure mode this architecture prevents.** Independent marts drift apart, and you end up with two departments quoting different revenue figures — **the information silo problem re-created inside the analytics layer.**

---

**Operational Data Store (ODS):**
- **An ODS consolidates data from multiple source systems and provides a near real-time integrated view of current data**
- **Its purpose is to provide data for operational purposes, and it has add, change or delete functionality**

**Advantages:** **overwrite function · save data at a document level · contains consolidated data · can be used for reporting and drill-down · designed to quickly perform relatively simple queries on small amounts of data**

**Differences from a data warehouse:**
- **An ODS stores only very recent information. In comparison, the data warehouse is more like long term memory, storing relatively permanent information**
- **In contrast to a data warehouse, data in ODS objects is stored in flat, transparent database tables. Fact and dimension tables are not created**

> **The ODS is the warehouse with two of its four characteristics deliberately reversed** — and stating *which* is the cleanest answer to "similarities and differences":

| Characteristic | **Data Warehouse** | **ODS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Integrated** | ✔ | ✔ **same** |
| **Subject-oriented** | ✔ star schemas | ✘ **flat, transparent tables — no facts or dimensions** |
| **Time-variant** | ✔ 5–10 years | ✘ **only very recent information** |
| **Non-volatile** | ✔ never overwritten | ✘ **overwrite function — add, change, delete** |

**They share integration and differ on everything else** — and each difference serves a different question:

$$\textbf{Warehouse: "what has been happening over years?"} \qquad \textbf{ODS: "what is true right now, across all systems?"}$$

**The ODS is the answer to data latency**, the warehouse's stated disadvantage. **If a call-centre agent needs the customer's current consolidated position, a warehouse refreshed nightly cannot help, and querying three source systems live is slow and fragile.**

⚠️ **"Overwrite function" is listed as an *advantage*, which is worth pausing on** — non-volatility was an advantage for the warehouse. **The same property is a virtue or a defect depending on the question: for history you must never overwrite; for *current state* you must.**

**And "save data at a document level" pairs with "relatively simple queries on small amounts of data"** — the ODS holds **individual documents**, not aggregates. **It answers *what happened to this one thing*, not *what is the trend*.**

---

**Data mining:**
- **Data mining is the process of extracting patterns from data, used in a wide range of uses such as marketing surveillance, fraud detection and scientific discovery**
- **Data Warehousing provides the enterprise with memory; Data Mining provides the enterprise with intelligence**
- **Data mining can discover valid, novel, potentially useful, and ultimately understandable patterns in data**

**Uses:** **customer analysis · targeted marketing · cross selling · segmenting or grouping customers · Market Basket Analysis · credit rating · fraud detection · medicine / disease outcome**

**Steps:** **Data Preparation → Model Construction → Results validation**

**Vendors — major players:** **Clementine · IBM's Intelligent Miner · SGI's MineSet · SAS's Enterprise Miner**; **others:** DataMind (NeurOagent) · Information Discovery (IDIS) · SAS Institute (SAS/Neuronets)

**The four properties of a mined pattern each rule out a specific failure:**

| Property | Rules out |
|---|---|
| **Valid** | a pattern that is **statistical noise** — true in this sample, false in general |
| **Novel** | a pattern you **already knew** — *"customers buy more at Diwali"* is true and useless |
| **Potentially useful** | a pattern you **cannot act on** |
| **Understandable** | a pattern **nobody can interpret or trust** |

> **Novelty is what distinguishes mining from reporting: reporting answers questions you asked; mining finds patterns you did not know to ask about.** That is exactly the deck's own contrast — *"warehousing provides memory; mining provides intelligence."*

⚠️ **Cautions needed while mining:** **search a large dataset for patterns and you will find some by pure chance.** That is why **"Results validation" is a named step, not an optional check** — **a pattern must be tested on data it was not discovered in.**

**Market Basket Analysis is the canonical example** — it finds **which products are bought together** from transaction data. **Its value is that it needs no theory:** nobody hypothesised the association; it fell out of the data. And it converts directly into action — **shelf placement, bundling, cross-sell recommendations.**

**How data mining is useful for CRM:**

| Mining use | CRM capability it powers |
|---|---|
| **Customer analysis · segmenting customers** | **customer segmentation and targeting** (marketing analytics) |
| **Targeted marketing** | **focused marketing** (CRM benefit) |
| **Cross selling · market basket analysis** | **better cross-sell / up-sell** (CRM benefit) |
| **Credit rating · fraud detection** | **credit checks, risk management** (FSCM, Unit 3) |

**Every CRM benefit that requires knowing something about a customer that they did not tell you is mining underneath.**

---

**Analytics:** **business applications that analyze data for specific business subjects — like Supply Chain, Customer Relationship Management, Human Resource, Finance.**

**Two major categories:** **descriptive analytics that focuses on history** *(historical customer patterns)* and **prescriptive analytics that focuses on trends to predict** *(customer's future behavior)*.

**Segments:** **① Financial and Business Performance Management (BPM)** — divided into **Financial Analytics** and **Business Performance Management** · **② CRM Analytics** · **③ Operations and Production Analytic Applications**

**The distinguishing feature is in the first line — *"for specific business subjects":***

$$\textbf{OLAP: a general tool} \qquad \textbf{Analytics: a packaged application for one function}$$

**An OLAP tool can slice any cube; a CRM analytics application already knows what a churn rate is.** The metrics, models and reports come pre-defined. **Which is why the three segments match the modules exactly** — Financial/BPM ↔ FI-CO, CRM Analytics ↔ CRM, Operations and Production ↔ PP and SCM.

⚠️ *(The deck uses **"prescriptive"** where **"predictive"** is the more standard term for *focuses on trends to predict*. Answer as the deck states it, and know that industry usually reads **descriptive** = what happened, **predictive** = what will happen, **prescriptive** = what should we do.)*

---

**Business Intelligence:**
- **Business intelligence tools mainly help in reporting as per the end user requirement**
- **OLAP, Analytics, Data mining etc. are part of the Business Intelligence suite**

**Functionalities of BI tools:** **alerts · scorecards · dashboards · ad hoc query · workflow · data delivery · customization of reports based on user profile · predictive modeling and data mining using advanced mathematical techniques · visualization · slice and dice of data**

**Leading vendors:** **SAP** *(SAP Business Intelligence is its flagship; **Business Objects** was taken over by SAP)* · **IBM Cognos** *(taken over by IBM)* · **Brio · Oracle · SAS Institute · Hyperion**

**BI is the umbrella:**

$$\textbf{BI} \supset \{\textbf{OLAP}, \textbf{Analytics}, \textbf{Data Mining}, \textbf{Reporting}\}$$

**So what does BI add on top of its parts?**

| Already in OLAP / mining | **BI adds** |
|---|---|
| slice and dice, visualization | **alerts** — the system tells *you* |
| ad hoc query | **scorecards, dashboards** — a curated standing view |
| predictive modeling and data mining | **workflow** — a finding triggers an action |
| | **data delivery**, **report customization by user profile** |

> **The additions all concern *pushing* rather than *pulling*.** OLAP waits for someone to ask a question. **Alerts, dashboards, scorecards, workflow and data delivery bring the answer to the person without them asking** — and route it onward when action is needed. **That is the difference between a tool and a system.**

**And the vendor list is another acquisition story, exactly like Unit 4's:** **Business Objects → SAP**, **Cognos → IBM**, **Hyperion → Oracle.** **Three independent BI leaders, all absorbed by suite vendors** — the *"specialists get acquired, suites get comprehensive"* half of Unit 3's arms race, in one line.

*(Market context from the deck's charts: the **Data Warehouse as a Service** market was **\$1.2 billion (2018-e)** growing to a projected **\$3.4 billion (2023-p)**, led by North America.)*

items.q: **Which processes are common across industries and which differ? Give examples of industry-exclusive processes for manufacturing industries, with the specialist ERPs for each.**
items.answer:
**Common processes across industries:**
- **Financial accounting**
- **Management accounting**
- **Corporate governance**
- **Human resource management processes — recruitment, payroll processing, talent management**
- **Corporate services like travel management**
- **Quality management**
- **Processes of global trade — import procedure, documentation, customs**
- **Managing some of the logistics functions like warehouse and transport management**

**Processes that differ across industries** — the deck's own contrast:
> *"An **oil and gas company** needs capabilities around **oil exploration** for finding new oil reserves, but that is not something important for a consumer goods company. In the same way, **product promotion** is an important feature for a consumer goods company to boost sales, however that may not make any sense for a petroleum company where **prices in countries like India are mostly dictated by government**."*

**The dividing line is precise:**

$$\textbf{common} = \textbf{how a company runs itself} \qquad \textbf{specific} = \textbf{what the company actually does}$$

**Every company pays people, keeps accounts, complies with law and moves goods** — which is exactly the set Unit 3 called *"across the whole enterprise"*. **The core operating process is where industries diverge.**

**And the deck's example pair is well chosen:** exploration matters only upstream; **promotion matters only where you set your own prices.** **A petroleum company in India cannot promote its way to more sales because the government fixes the price** — so the feature is not merely unused, it is meaningless.

> **That is the commercial basis of the whole industry-solution market**, and why *"industry specific functionality"* can override an entire package-selection process in Unit 4.

---

**Oil and gas — industry-specific processes:** **exploration · developing petroleum fields · managing refinery operations · lubes manufacturing operations · oil and gas commodity trading · managing bulk transport of inflammable materials and hydrocarbon products · terminals management · service station operations / fuel management · convenience retailing**

**Oil industry specific ERPs: Aspentech · SAP IS-Oil**

**The value chain:**
$$\textbf{Upstream} \rightarrow \textbf{Mid-Stream} \rightarrow \textbf{Refining} \rightarrow \textbf{Primary Distribution Network} \rightarrow \textbf{Secondary Distribution Network} \rightarrow \textbf{Service Station Retailing}$$
with product streams **Crude · Refined Products & LPG · Lubes · Natural Gas** spanning different segments.

**The integrated supply chain slide expands it:** **Crude Oil / NG → Refinery → Pipelines → Terminal → Station → Industrial Customer / Reseller**, with activities **Select/Acquire Crude → Refine Crude → Optimize Product Mix → Move Products → Store Products → Replenish Products → Sell Products**.

**The distinctive thing about oil is that one company spans the whole chain from a hole in the ground to a petrol pump** — and the process list reads that chain end to end.

**"Optimize Product Mix" has no equivalent in discrete manufacturing.** A refinery does not choose to make petrol *or* diesel — **one barrel of crude yields a whole slate of products simultaneously**, and the optimisation is choosing **which slate** to run given current prices for every output. *(Which is why **Aspentech**, described earlier as "strong in Process Industry", is named here.)*

⚠️ **Two entries on the SAP Oil & Gas solution map are genuinely industry-exclusive:**
- **Joint Venture Management** — oil fields are **too expensive and risky for one company**, so they are developed by consortia. **Costs and revenues must be split among partners** by share, with statements to each. **No generic ERP has this.**
- **Exchange & Throughput Handling** — oil companies **swap product with competitors** rather than transport it. *You give me a tanker in Chennai; I give you one in Mumbai.* **Both save the freight.** **A transaction type that exists in essentially no other industry.**

---

**Automotive:** **Kanban planning / scheduling for multiple models in an assembly line · Warranty Management · Just in sequence deliveries by suppliers directly to assembly line · Managing vehicle information and vehicle life cycle · Managing Dealer Business · Car Leasing**

**"Just in sequence" is JIT taken one step further:**

$$\textbf{JIT: the right parts at the right time} \qquad \textbf{JIS: in the order the line will use them}$$

On a line building **multiple models mixed together**, the seats for car 47 must arrive **immediately before car 47 reaches the seat station** — not a pallet of assorted seats. **The supplier must sequence their delivery to your production sequence, which requires seeing your line schedule in near real time. That is the deepest possible supply-chain collaboration — beyond VMI, beyond CPFR.**

**"Managing vehicle information and life cycle" is distinctive because the *individual unit* matters** — a car maker tracks **this specific car** by VIN, through manufacture, sale, service, warranty claims and resale. **Which is why warranty management and dealer business are on the same list.** *(And "car leasing" shows the manufacturer becoming a financial services business too.)*

---

**Pharmaceutical:** **Patent Management · Managing Intellectual Property · Clinical trial management · Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) · Secure Tracing and Tracking / E-Pedigree · Product / Patient Safety Regulatory Compliance Submission · Secrecy of Formulation**

**Every process exists because of one of two pressures:**

| Pressure | Processes |
|---|---|
| **Regulation** | clinical trial management · LIMS · **E-Pedigree** · regulatory compliance submission |
| **Intellectual property** | patent management · managing IP · **secrecy of formulation** |

**E-Pedigree is the sharpest:** an electronic record of **every custody transfer a drug pack has undergone**, from manufacturer to pharmacy, existing to **defeat counterfeit medicines** entering the legitimate supply chain. **It is a legal requirement, not a business choice.**

> **That is batch management from Unit 3 taken to its logical end.** Batch tracking answered *"which batch is this?"*; **e-pedigree answers *"who has held this specific pack, and when?"***

**"Secrecy of formulation" constrains the ERP's own design.** In pharma **the formulation *is* the asset**, so the system must let people plan and buy against a recipe **without letting them see it** — the material-master access principle at maximum strictness.

*(And **LIMS** is a named interface in Unit 4's interface-scope list: **the instruments produce the test results; the ERP cannot release the batch without them.**)*

---

**Consumer goods:** **strong distribution planning capability · promotion planning / trade promotions · brand management · managing large number of SKUs · manufacturing outsourcing / contract manufacturing · collaboration with retailers · route management · Direct Store Delivery (DSD) · food safety · managing cold chain (fresh foods) · managing empties and returns (beverage) · markdowns (apparel) · managing fashion, style, design (apparel)**

**This list is the mineral-water question answered** — for consumer goods, **the product is cheap and the supply chain is everything**, which is why **nine of the thirteen processes are distribution, logistics or retail collaboration.**

**Direct Store Delivery is the distinctive one:** the manufacturer's own vehicle delivers **straight to each shop**, bypassing the retailer's DC — used for products that are **perishable, high-frequency or need shelf servicing.** **It gives the manufacturer control of the shelf and costs them a delivery fleet**, which is why *route management* sits beside it.

**And "collaboration with retailers" is where this unit's own VMI and CPFR live** — **Wal-Mart and P&G** was precisely a consumer-goods-to-retailer collaboration. **This industry is the reason those techniques exist.**

---

**Mining:** **safety · handling hazardous materials (explosives) · managing logistics at remote locations · transport optimization · washing / beneficiation · blending · commodity pricing · commodity auctions · Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) · exploration**

**Mining-specific ERPs: SAP IS-Mine · Mincom · Gemcom**

⚠️ **Two entries are unusual enough to remember.** **"Washing / Beneficiation"** raises the grade of extracted ore by removing waste rock — **peculiar from an ERP standpoint because the input is variable in quality and the output quantity is not fixed.** You cannot write a BOM saying *one tonne of ore yields X tonnes of concentrate*. **Blending** then combines ores of different grades to hit a target specification. **Both are process-industry recipes with variable yield, which no discrete BOM can express.**

**"Corporate Social Responsibility" appearing as a *process* is striking.** Mining operates in remote communities under intense scrutiny; **CSR commitments — local employment, community investment, rehabilitation — are contractual conditions of the mining licence**, so they must be tracked and reported like any other obligation. **It is compliance, not philanthropy.**

*(**Mincom** was named in Unit 4 as an example of a package *"strong in a particular industry"* — **Mincom in Mining.** Same fact, other direction.)*

items.q: **Give examples of industry-exclusive processes for service industries — retail, healthcare, education, banking, insurance and utilities — with the main components of a retail ERP solution.**
items.answer:
**Retail — industry-specific processes:** **category management · merchandise budgeting and planning · assortment management · space management · advanced promotion planning functionality and planning markdowns · store clustering · specialized retail replenishment functionalities like continuous replenishment, cross docking · point of sales solutions · cross channel order fulfilment · store operations**

**Main components of a retail ERP solution:** **master data · merchandise planning, procurement and replenishment · supply chain execution · managing pricing and promotions · point of sale integration · reports / KPIs / exception alerts · store operations · retail planning**

**Retail ERPs: Retek · JDA · SAP IS-Retail**

**Retail's processes are all about *what to stock, where, and at what price* — because a retailer makes nothing:**

| Process | The decision it makes |
|---|---|
| **Category management** | how do we manage **a whole category** as a business? |
| **Assortment management** | **which items** should this store carry? |
| **Space management** | **how much shelf** does each item get? |
| **Store clustering** | which stores are **similar enough** to treat the same way? |
| **Merchandise budgeting** | **how much money** into which category? |
| **Promotion planning and markdowns** | **what price**, when? |

> **Store clustering is what makes the others tractable.** A chain with 800 stores cannot plan an assortment for each, and a single national assortment ignores that a city-centre store and a highway store sell different things. **Clustering makes assortment and space decisions per cluster — a few dozen decisions instead of 800.** *(The same "match the resolution to the decision" principle as ABC classification and rough-cut capacity planning.)*

**"Cross channel order fulfilment" is the modern requirement** — order online collect in store, buy in store deliver home, return anywhere. **It demands a single view of inventory across every store and warehouse.**

⚠️ **The Oracle Retek product list is worth noting because it is this entire course, re-badged for retail:**

| Retek product | What it is |
|---|---|
| **RETL** — Retail Extract, Transform and Load | **ETL** |
| **Retail Data Warehouse** | **the data warehouse** |
| **RDF** — Retail Demand Forecasting | **demand planning** |
| **AIP** — Advanced Inventory Planning | **inventory models** |
| **RWMS** — Retail Warehouse Management | **supply chain execution** |
| **ReIM** — Retail Invoice Matching | **three-way matching** |
| **RIB** — Retail Integration Bus | **EAI** |
| **VCC** — Value Chain Collaboration | **CPFR / VMI** |

> **An industry solution is not different technology — it is the same technology with the industry's vocabulary, data model and processes pre-configured.** *(Which is also the honest answer to what you are buying: **pre-configuration, not novelty** — the same idea as **preconfigured templates** for SMBs in Unit 4.)*

---

**Healthcare — for providers:** **managing medical records · scheduling appointments · planning for beds · managing operation theatre · tracking of inpatients and outpatients · managing waiting lists of patients · patient help desk and managing patient queries · providing information and education to patients · online diagnostic reporting / image reports**

**For payers:** **claims handling · payer relationship management · payer communication**

**ERP modules for a hospital:** **patient management · scheduling (bed, OT, appointments) · patient help desk · pharmacy · pathology · store · payroll · accounts and billing · patient online investigation reports · hospital MIS / reports**

**The provider's process layers:** **Core processes** — *Prevent* (manage health programs, advise healthy lifestyles), *Diagnose* (order tests, execute tests, analyze information), *Treat* (prescribe medication, execute surgery, provide treatment), *Care/Support* (nursing care, home care, chronic illness) · **Manage Resources** — human resources, operation theatres, materials, diagnostic appliances, beds, outpatient rooms, medications, tools, **organs, blood** · **Manage Information** — patient info, appointments, medical reports, physical records, doctor's info · **Support processes** — finance & cost, purchasing, logistics, HR, IT

**The provider/payer split is the structural insight:**

$$\textbf{Provider: delivers care} \qquad \textbf{Payer: pays for it}$$

**They are different organisations with different systems**, and *"Payer Relationship Management"* is literally **CRM where the customer is an insurer.**

⚠️ **The "Manage Resources" list contains the most striking entry in the chapter: *"organs, blood."*** **These are inventory items** — stock level, location, expiry, matching requirement. But they are **perishable in hours, non-substitutable, and impossible to reorder.** No procurement lead time applies; no EOQ can be calculated. **It is the extreme case of the critical-item quadrant — *"should never be out of stock"* — with no way to guarantee supply.**

**Scheduling is the other hard problem** — *bed planning, operation theatre, waiting lists* are **finite-capacity scheduling against uncertain demand**, except that the "orders" are patients, arrivals are partly emergencies, and **you cannot hold inventory of treated patients.** **An empty operating theatre hour is gone forever, exactly like an unsold hotel room** — which is Unit 3's caution about services made concrete.

---

**Educational institutions:** **student master data · registration / admission to different study programs · handling different examinations · managing students' performance and grading · managing student financials · online services to students**, plus **managing education campuses · managing libraries**, and **academic services** — *planning courses and curriculum, developing course content, scheduling class/exam and publishing schedules, planning capacities, evaluation of different programs.*

**Modules:** **Admission · Registration · Grading · Progression · Degree · Graduation · Financial Aid · Alumni Relations**

$$\textbf{Admission} \rightarrow \textbf{Registration} \rightarrow \textbf{Grading} \rightarrow \textbf{Progression} \rightarrow \textbf{Degree} \rightarrow \textbf{Graduation} \rightarrow \textbf{Alumni Relations}$$

> **This is the fourth life-cycle module in the course** — **Hire-to-Retire** for employees, **lead-to-repeat-customer** for customers, **concept-to-retirement** for products, and now **admission-to-alumni** for students. **Every one: take a long-lived entity, follow it end to end, hold one record across every function.**

**And "Alumni Relations" after graduation is the giveaway that this is CRM in disguise** — the relationship continues after the "transaction" completes, exactly the **Customer → Account → Repeat** transition.

---

**Banking:**

| Group | Processes |
|---|---|
| **Normal banking** | **savings account and card transactions · fixed term deposit · shares, bonds, investment funds, derivatives · brokerage services · card management** |
| **Financing services** | **loans to customers · project financing · trade financing / Letter of Credit (LOC) · leasing** |
| **Treasury management** | **interest rate management · foreign exchange management / trading currencies · credit risk management** |

**Leading banking ERPs: Finacle (Infosys) · FLEXCUBE (Oracle) · IS-Banking (SAP) · BaNCS (TCS)**

⚠️ **Banking is the one industry where the ERP's *core* is finance rather than production** — and that inverts the usual architecture. **In a manufacturer, FI-CO *records* what production and sales did. In a bank, the financial transaction *is* the product.** There is no factory; **the ledger is the operation.**

**That is why banking ERPs are a completely separate product category with their own vendors** rather than a configuration of SAP's standard ERP. **Two of the four named are Indian: Finacle by Infosys and BaNCS by TCS.**

**And note that "treasury management" appears here as a *core banking process*** while in Unit 3 it was one of four categories of the finance module. **Same function, utterly different weight** — for a manufacturer treasury manages spare cash; **for a bank, interest rate, FX and credit risk management are the business.**

---

**Insurance — the ERP solution comprises:** **Customer Relationship Management · Product & Service Configuration · Policy Management · Commissions Mgmt · Claims Management · Inkasso / Exkasso (Collections & Disbursements) · Cash Management · Investment Management · Management Accounting · Financial Accounting · General Ledger · Reporting · Profitability Analysis · Human Resources · Facility Maintenance · Procurement · Overhead Mgmt** — accessed through **Internet · Agency · Interaction Center**

**It puts CRM and the Interaction Center at the front and Policy, Claims and Commissions in the middle.** **Insurance is a relationship business with two moments of truth — selling the policy and paying the claim** — and *Inkasso/Exkasso* is money flowing in as premiums and out as claims. **The whole business is those two flows.**

---

**Utilities:** **managing meters** *(installation and inspection of meters; reading meters and consumption determination)* **· energy trading · billing · managing waste and emission**

**Utilities are distinctive because of scale and because the "order" is continuous.** A utility has **millions of customers**, each consuming continuously rather than placing orders. **There is no sales order, no delivery, no goods issue** — there is a **meter**, and consumption is discovered by reading it.

$$\textbf{meter reading} \rightarrow \textbf{consumption determination} \rightarrow \textbf{billing}$$

**That three-step chain replaces the entire Order-to-Cash cycle**, and is why **billing is named as a process in its own right** — producing millions of accurate bills from millions of readings on a cycle is a genuinely large task.

**"Energy trading" is the same commodity logic as oil; "managing waste and emission" is the regulatory obligation**, matching **EHS** from Unit 3 and **product safety** from PLM. *(And **Ramco** was named in Unit 4 as *"Ramco for Utilities"* — the industry-specific package example, closing the loop with the selection chapter.)*

items.q: **Explain cloud computing and its advantages. Explain software as a service — its characteristics, benefits and drivers. How is hosted ERP different from SaaS, and what are the major issues in putting ERP on SaaS?**
items.answer:
**Cloud computing:**
- **Cloud computing ensures that a company need not invest in the hardware upfront for deploying a business application like ERP, and can pay for it based on usage — i.e. computing infrastructure is available on demand**
- **Thus cloud computing is a way of computing, via internet**
- **Cloud computing customers do not own the physical infrastructure, thus avoiding capital expenditure by renting usage from a third-party provider and paying only for what they use**

**Areas of cloud computing:** **Database as a service · Desktop as a service · Disaster recovery as a service · Infrastructure as a service · Integration as a service · Platform as a service · Storage as a service**

**Advantages:** **cost reduction · improvement in efficiency and utilization · centralization of infrastructure · individual companies need not design the hardware based on peak load · scalability · easier maintenance · better reliability · measuring resource usage · infrastructure available anytime anywhere**

**Disadvantages / the criticism:**
> *"Critics against cloud theory remark that although companies might be able to **save on upfront capital expenditures, they might not save much and might actually pay more for operating expenses**. So **in situations where the capital expense is relatively small, the cloud model may not make great financial sense**."*

**The single most important advantage is the one stated as a full sentence: *"individual companies need not design the hardware based on peak load."***

**On premise, you must buy for the peak.** If your month-end close needs four times the capacity of an ordinary day, **you own four times the hardware and it idles for twenty-nine days a month.**

$$\textbf{on-premise capacity} = \textbf{peak demand} \qquad \textbf{cloud capacity} = \textbf{current demand}$$

**And this is why *centralization of infrastructure* and *improvement in efficiency and utilization* are separate advantages:** the provider **pools many customers whose peaks fall at different times, so the same physical hardware serves everyone's peak** without anyone owning idle capacity.

> **This is precisely the capacity-planning problem from Unit 3** — *"organizations have defined resources / limited capacity… customer needs fluctuate… a mismatch results in under-utilization or overload."* **Cloud is the answer to that for computing capacity: it converts a fixed resource into a variable one.**

**The criticism is a genuine argument, not a hedge.** Cloud converts **CapEx into OpEx** — you stop buying hardware and start paying rent. **Rent never stops.** Over a long enough horizon, for a **steady, predictable load**, owning is cheaper. **So: cloud wins where demand is variable or unpredictable; ownership wins where it is steady and large.**

*(The seven "as a service" areas read as layers: **IaaS** rents servers/storage/network · **PaaS** adds OS and middleware · **SaaS** rents the whole application. **Each layer up rents more and controls less.**)*

---

**Software as a Service — the QnA's model answer:**

- **With SaaS, a provider licenses an application to customers for use as a service on demand, through time subscription or "pay-as-you-use" model**
- **This model allows vendors to develop, host and operate software for customer use**
- **Rather than purchase the hardware and software to run an application, customers need only a computer or a server to download the application, and internet access to run the software**
- **SaaS vendors can adopt different approaches for giving customers access — they may host the application on their own web servers, or upload the application to the consumer device and disable it after the contract expires**
- **While SaaS was widely deployed initially for sales force automation (SFA) and Customer Relationship Management (CRM), it gradually became popular for computerized billing, invoicing, HR management, service desk management, sales pipeline management etc.**

**SaaS characteristics:**
1. **Network based access to a business software**
2. **Activities (like maintenance) are managed from a central location rather than at each customer's site**
3. **SaaS application delivery follows a one-to-many model**
4. **Generally SaaS vendors price applications on a per-user basis, mostly with a minimum number of users and with additional fees for extra bandwidth and storage**

**SaaS Benefits:** **saves money as the entire cost is variable with no fixed cost or upfront investment — easy to calculate ROI · multi-tenant efficiency, as the software is used by multiple companies so it is never idle · faster releases of new features, since the entire community benefits · flexibility and scalability**

**SaaS Drivers:** **growth of adoption of package applications / ERPs by SMBs · computing has become a commodity · SaaS is more popular for applications that are more standard across industries · more matured software evolution · software hosting capability had matured over years · network, bandwidth and security becoming more reliable**

> **"One-to-many" is the characteristic that generates all the others, and naming it is the strongest answer:**

$$\textbf{one instance of the software} \longrightarrow \textbf{many customers}$$

| Because it is one-to-many… | …this follows |
|---|---|
| maintenance happens once | **"managed from a central location rather than at each customer's site"** |
| everyone is on the same version | **"faster releases — the entire community benefits"** |
| hardware is shared across customers | **"multi-tenant efficiency — never idle"** |
| **you cannot change shared code** | **customization is impossible** |

**The last row is the cost, and it is not a limitation of the technology — it is a direct consequence of the model.** You cannot modify software that a thousand other companies are simultaneously running.

**And *"SaaS became popular for applications that are more standard across industries"* is that constraint stated as market behaviour.** Payroll, expenses, service desk and CRM are similar everywhere, so a standard version fits. **Manufacturing, industry-specific processes and complex finance are not** — which is exactly why ERP was late to SaaS. *(Note where SaaS started: **SFA and CRM** — matching the CRM vendor quadrant, where Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive and Zoho lead, all SaaS-native.)*

---

**Hosted ERP:**
- **The ERP application can be hosted in a service provider's data center**
- **Hosting ERP is becoming popular among customers looking to outsource their existing ERP implementations to avoid capital outlays, and customers lacking access to knowledgeable ERP staff**
- **Leading ERPs like SAP and Oracle are looking at hosting as a possible source of new revenue for managed services, beyond traditional license revenue**

**Differences from SaaS:**
- **ERP hosting is typically done for a particular customer — it does not follow the multi-tenant architecture of SaaS**
- **Under SaaS the same standard software must be used by all tenants and no modification in custom code or configuration is possible — in hosted ERP, code modification or customization is possible as per the customer's requirement**
- **Unlike SaaS where the customer pays a monthly subscription fee (and does not own the license), in hosting customers pay a license fee (and they own the license)**
- **In SaaS the software vendor decides when to upgrade; in hosting the customer decides on upgrade timing and whether to upgrade at all**

**The comparison table:**

| Criteria | **SaaS** | **Hosted ERP** |
|---|---|---|
| **Architecture** | **Multi Tenant** | **Single Tenant** |
| **Fee Structure** | **Subscription based** | **License** |
| **License ownership** | **ERP Vendor** | **Customer** |
| **Customization / code modification** | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Application hosting — who?** | **ERP vendor's data center** | **Service provider's data center** |
| **Application upgrade — who?** | **ERP vendor** | **Customer** |
| **Application and infrastructure maintenance — who?** | **ERP vendor / software publisher** | **Service provider** |

> **All seven rows follow from row one — multi-tenant versus single-tenant:**

$$\textbf{Multi-tenant: one instance, many customers} \qquad \textbf{Single-tenant: one instance, one customer}$$

| Because SaaS is multi-tenant… | Because hosting is single-tenant… |
|---|---|
| **no customization** — cannot modify shared code | **customization possible** — it is your instance |
| **vendor decides upgrades** — everyone moves together | **customer decides**, or never upgrades |
| **vendor hosts and maintains** | **a service provider** hosts your copy |
| **subscription, vendor owns the licence** | **you own the licence** |

**The upgrade row has the sharpest practical consequence.** Under SaaS you **cannot refuse an upgrade** — unsettling for a company running its operations on it, **but it also means you can never fall behind and never face the *"large amount of customization ⇒ the system cannot evolve"* death spiral from Unit 4.** **The constraint that removes your control also removes your ability to make that mistake.**

**For which type of customer is hosted ERP a good option?** The deck answers it: **customers outsourcing an existing implementation to avoid capital outlays, and customers lacking knowledgeable ERP staff.** In other words — **you have already customised, you already own the licence, and you cannot go to SaaS; but you do not want to run the data centre. Hosting is the middle position.**

---

**Major issues in putting ERP on SaaS:**
- **Security of customer specific data**
- **Ensuring a high level of availability of the ERP system, as ERP is the heart of the company's business operations**
- **Each customer needs specific customization, and it is difficult to stick to a standard solution**

**Special capabilities needed from a service provider:**
- **A very thorough understanding of how the software is being used by the client base**
- **The ability to maintain and upgrade the software remotely**
- **Ensuring high system availability — virtually no downtime is acceptable**

⚠️ **The third issue is fundamental, and it is a contradiction rather than a difficulty:** **SaaS requires a standard solution; ERP customers need industry-specific and company-specific configuration.**

**The deck's own resolution is the interesting part:** *"success of ERP / CRM software as SaaS will depend on offering the capability of offering **industry best-practice configurations**, as well as the ability for the customer to do **further configuration**."*

> **That is the preconfigured-template idea from Unit 4 made into the enabling condition for SaaS ERP — configuration, not code.** Let customers configure within the standard; never let them modify it. **The distinction between configuration and customization, which mattered commercially in Unit 4, becomes architecturally load-bearing here.**

**And the reality check:** per **Panorama Consulting's 2013 ERP Report**, **on-premise ERP was still 61%**, with **SaaS 14%**, **Cloud ERP 12%** and **Other 13%**. **The emerging trends were, at the time, genuinely emerging.**

items.q: **Define SOA. What is a service and what are its properties? What are the fundamental principles and benefits of SOA? What is RFID — its components, advantages and disadvantages over bar code, and benefits? How do EAI applications benefit business and why is the hub model better than point-to-point? How does ERP II make ERPs more powerful?**
items.answer:
**A service:**
- **Services refer to the building blocks — the containers in which the data and programs from ERP, CRM, and so on are collected for use in creating new systems**
- **These building blocks can be understood both by business executives and IT staff, because each of these services is actually a business function**
- **Web Services are the building block for service-oriented architecture. These services are functional building-blocks accessible over standard Internet protocols, independent of platforms and programming languages**
- **All leading ERP vendors have started building a repository of enterprise services for the business processes they offer**

**Advantages of a service: re-usability · easy integration**
