> **The defining phrase is *"each of these services is actually a business function."*** A service is not a technical routine — it is something like ***"check credit"***, ***"create sales order"***, ***"post goods receipt."* That is what makes it understood by both business and IT**, and what makes composing services into processes a **business** activity rather than a programming one.

$$\textbf{business function} \equiv \textbf{callable service}$$

**And *"independent of platforms and programming languages"* is what makes it work across vendors** — a service exposed by SAP can be called by a .NET application. **That property is what lets an enterprise assemble a process from pieces of different systems.**

---

**Service Oriented Architecture:**
- **SOA is a flexible set of design principles used during system development and integration**
- **SOA relies on a mesh of software services which are loosely coupled and can be combined to build any business process application**
- **SOA defines how to integrate widely disparate applications for a world that is Web based and can use multiple platforms from different vendors — SAP (NetWeaver), Oracle, IBM (WebSphere), Microsoft (.Net)**
- **SOA helps build large applications from existing software services, reducing programming and testing to a bare minimum, as these web services are already tested**

**SOA principles:** **re-usability · modularity · composability · componentization · interoperability · loose coupling · standards-compliance**

**SOA benefits:**
- **Helps businesses respond more quickly and cost-effectively to changing market conditions**
- **Promotes reuse — what has been developed can be reused, saving time and cost**
- **Dramatically simplified testing, as services are independently fully tested by the vendor who publishes them, with full documentation of interfaces**
- **Application integration savings**
- **Because interfaces are platform-independent, a client from any device using any OS in any coding language can access or use the service**
- **SOA opens up opportunities for thousands of small niche vendors who have specialized knowledge in a particular business process — they can build applications quickly integrated with SAP or Oracle, giving them a larger market**

**The seven principles are really three ideas:**

| Idea | Principles |
|---|---|
| **Break it into pieces** | **modularity · componentization** |
| **Make the pieces fit together** | **composability · interoperability · standards-compliance** |
| **Keep the pieces independent** | **loose coupling · re-usability** |

**Loose coupling is the load-bearing one** — it means a service can be **changed or replaced without breaking its callers**, because they depend on its *interface*, not its internals. **Without loose coupling, "composable" services become a tangle that cannot be changed.**

⚠️ **The last benefit is the most strategically interesting and easy to skim past:** *"SOA opens up opportunities for **thousands of small niche vendors**… now they can build applications quickly integrated with SAP or Oracle."* **That is a market-structure claim, not a technical one. By making integration cheap, SOA lowers the barrier to entry for specialists** — which is part of why **best-of-breed remained viable** against the suites, and precisely Unit 3's *"the specialized products are getting specialized further."*

---

**RFID — technology components:**

**Tags** — **affixed to objects; information is written to an embedded chip.** **Active** = **includes a power source to help transmit a signal**; **Passive** = **no power to transmit; relies on readers**
**Reader** — **emits a radio signal via an antenna**
**Antenna** — **device attached to a reader which helps transmit radio signals and capture "scan" readings**

**How it operates:** **tags can be read remotely when they detect a radio frequency signal from a reader over a range of distances; readers then either send tag information to back-end systems for processing or display it to the end user.**

**Advantages over traditional bar code:**
1. **RFID's most talked about advantage is that it does not require a line of sight between reader and tag.** In case of bar code, **each item must be presented to the scanner in a particular orientation and brought sufficiently close**
2. **RFID tags can hold lots of data — up to hundreds of characters — whereas bar codes can store only 12–15 digits**
3. **RFID tags can be rewritten thousands of times, whereas bar codes can be printed only once.** **At different nodes of the supply chain — factory, warehouse — data can be continuously added, which is not possible for a bar code: once printed it is frozen**
4. **Manual labor associated with reading bar-code data is reduced, because the RFID scanning device can gather data automatically from items kept deep inside boxes**

**Disadvantages:**
- **Bar codes have reached a high level of maturity, whereas RFID needs to stabilize on standards**
- **The main barrier of RFID technology is the cost of the tag**

**Each advantage removes a different constraint:**

| Advantage | Constraint removed |
|---|---|
| **No line of sight** | **a human must handle each item** |
| **Hundreds of characters vs 12–15 digits** | **the tag can only identify, not describe** |
| **Rewritable thousands of times** | **the label is frozen at printing** |

**The first is transformative** — an **entire pallet can be read as it passes through a doorway** instead of being unpacked and scanned one by one. **That converts goods receipt from a manual task into an automatic event**, which is why Unit 4's GR process listed *"bar codes, RFID — simpler, faster process."*

**The third is the subtle one:** because a tag is **rewritable**, data can be **added at each node** — the factory writes the batch, the warehouse the location, the distributor the shipment. **The tag accumulates a history that travels with the object** — exactly what **e-pedigree** requires.

$$\textbf{bar code: an identifier} \qquad \textbf{RFID tag: a travelling record}$$

⚠️ **The two disadvantages are honest and decisive.** Standards immaturity is **temporary**; **tag cost is structural** — a bar code is printed ink and costs essentially nothing. **Which is why RFID spread at pallet and case level long before item level: apply the expensive control where the value justifies it.**

**RFID benefits in the supply chain**, across **Manufacturer Plant → Manufacturer DC → Retailer DC → Retail Store**: **tracking of items · reduced shrinkage · better replenishment · efficient reverse logistics · improved inventory, receiving, and shipping accuracy.**

**Every one is a Unit 4 KPI improved** — **shrinkage**, **cycle counting accuracy**, **stock outs**, **inventory turn** — **and improved accuracy has knock-on value, because the whole inventory pyramid runs on the control layer's numbers.**

---

**Enterprise Application Integration (EAI):**
- **EAI is an integration framework composed of a collection of technologies and services that form a middleware to enable integration of systems and applications across the enterprise**
- **EAI needs to link various applications that reside on different operating systems, use different database solutions and different computer languages**

**Leading EAI products:** **IBM (WebSphere Business Integration) · Microsoft (BizTalk Server) · SAP (NetWeaver Process Integration — PI) · Oracle (Fusion Middleware) · Sterling Commerce · Tibco Software**

**Why the hub model beats point-to-point — the arithmetic is the answer:**

With **point-to-point**, every pair of systems that must talk needs its own interface. For $n$ systems:

$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \textbf{ interfaces} \qquad\text{versus}\qquad n \textbf{ interfaces with a hub}$$

| Systems | **Point-to-point** | **Hub** |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | **10** | **5** |
| 10 | **45** | **10** |
| 20 | **190** | **20** |

**The gap widens quadratically**, and the maintenance burden widens with it: **in point-to-point, changing one system's format means changing every interface that touches it; in a hub, you change one connection.**

> **And EAI is what makes ERP II possible** — *"ERPs now can be integrated with best-of-breed vendors seamlessly **with one interface**"* is a named driver, **and "with one interface" is precisely the hub model.** Without it, the co-existence of ERP, CRM, SRM, SCP and PLM that this whole course describes would be unmanageable.

*(Note that **SOA and EAI answer the same problem from two directions:** **EAI is middleware that connects existing applications**; **SOA is a design principle that makes applications connectable in the first place.** SAP's **NetWeaver PI** appears as an EAI product and **NetWeaver** as an SOA platform — the same family serving both.)*

---

**How ERP II makes ERPs more powerful:**
- **ERP's focus was totally enterprise-centric and focused on internal resource optimization and transactional processing. ERP II has a new focus on process integration and external collaboration**
- **Collaborative commerce with suppliers and customers is the heart of ERP II**
- **ERP II also showed the strength of the internet. Applications like SRM, CRM and PLM today depend much on the internet for most of their functionalities**

**Major drivers for the journey from ERP to ERP II:**
1. **ERPs are extending outside the organization**
2. **ERPs now can be accessed from anywhere anytime**
3. **ERP now can be integrated with best-of-breed vendors seamlessly with one interface**

> **The three drivers are the three technologies of this topic, one each:**

| Driver | Technology |
|---|---|
| **extending outside the organization** | **SOA and web services** — cross-company process composition |
| **accessed from anywhere anytime** | **mobile, internet, cloud** |
| **integrated with best-of-breed with one interface** | **EAI** |

**That is why these technologies are taught together — they are not a miscellany of trends but the specific enablers that turned ERP into ERP II.**

$$\textbf{ERP: internal resource optimization} \longrightarrow \textbf{ERP II: process integration and external collaboration}$$

**And on mobile specifically** — the deck's advantages: **very useful for sales or service/maintenance staff who remain in the field and for whom it is difficult to come to office** · **quick real-time service to customers** · **increased productivity — access to all customer information and past transactions while visiting** · **simpler life for maintenance crews** · **extra high service for special customers where service is a differentiator**. **Typical M-Business transactions: inventory management · price check · supply chain management · stock management · customer service · payment via mobile phone · product ordering.**

**The multi-channel diagram is what ERP II looks like in practice:** the same back-end ERP reached through **mobile** *(sales staff pull info; field staff get their next job on a PDA)*, **internet** *(a customer order creates a back-end order)*, **contact centre** *(a phone service request creates a service order)*, and **VPN**. **The system did not change; the number of doors into it did.**
